title: Content We Liked: 27th September 2026
content:
Although it’s a big internet out there, the Tabletop digital universe is pretty small and spread out. In Content We Liked, we take a look at the articles, videos, podcasts, and products that caught our eyes or were noteworthy during the prior week you might have missed.

On the Internet at Large

Bitz Box Chaos Spawn by love2pronk

Welcome back to Content We Liked! We've got a surreal end to your September this week, with a trio of wonderfully strange entries starting with these Chaos Spawn by love2pronk on Bluesky. This pair of lil' weirdos come form the fine hobby tradition of finding spare parts in your bitz box and stapling them together to see what comes out. Its a damn fine tradition and these spawn are a gleaming example of the art.

Plaguebearers by wolfliche

Next up on our cavalcade of strange lil' dudes we've got some very out of the ordinary Plaguebearers from wolfliche on Instagram. One part oldhammer margin critter, one part mythos creature, these Plaguebearers are far outside what you'd expect of the concept but really, really work for something a little beyond mortal comprehension. And to think they're all made out of beads, that's some fine hobbying there.

The Biotransference of The Necrons by the warsinger

Last up for this week's edition we have a spectacular diorama piece by CWL favourite the warsinger, depicting The Biotransference of the Necrontyr into the souless Necrons. We're not gonna waste time, click through and look at it for yourself. This is an incredible piece and deserves your eyesballs on it.

This Week on Tabletop Battles

Tabletop Battles Reviews: Warhammer Tone Pro Paints

Games Workshop set up a whole hulaballoo the other week when they announced Tone Pro, their new expansion to the Citadel Warhammer paint range promising better coverage, vibrancy and flexible triads. Rob and Cronch take a look at some sample packs of the new range and put it through its paces.

Warhammer Tone Pro Paint Review

Warhammer, Death Metal and the Midlands: An Interview with Ash Moore of Mutagenic Host

Saelfe brings us a lovely little chat with Ash Moore, vocalist for Death Metal group Mutagenic Host, talking Warhammer, Metal and the Midlands of England over a game of Age of Sigmar.

An Interview with Ash Moore of Mutagenic Host

Ruleshammer 11th Edition: Orks

Ruleshammer deepdives the new Ork Codex looking at common questions and tricky rules interactions.

Ruleshammer 11th Edition: Orks

Tabletop Battles Reviews Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave

Friend of the site Elly joins us for their first full piece with a review of Fortune's Weave, the latest installment of the staggeringly popular Tactical RPG and sometimes dating sim Fire Emblem.

Tabletop Battles Reviews Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave

Turn Order: What Is Cyberpunk Red, and Why Should You Play It?

King Ghidra lifts the lid on Cyberpunk Red, the tabletop RPG behind Cyberpunk Edgerunners and 2077, and explains why you should give it a try.

Turn Order: What Is Cyberpunk Red, and Why Should You Play It?

Subscriber Exclusives Roundup

Isaac gives you the best practices and advice on dealing with the overtuned Ork codex, Floof talks about how they play Rad-Zone Cohort, and Innes Wilson joins us to run through some of the more interesting units from Codex Space Marines.

title: Check out the new Custodes models for Warhammer 40k in their golden glory
content:
Warhammer 40,000 is known for a lot of words that start with the letter G. God-Emperor, grimdark, guns, and of course, gratuitous gore. But there's another word that always comes to mind when I see the Ten Thousand standing regally upon Terra's holy ground: Golden.  In this week's Sunday Preview for Warhammer 40k, fans can check out the God-Emperor's favorite guys and gals in all their shiny glory.

The Adeptus Custodes have always been among my favorite Warhammer 40k factions. For all the supposed overpoweredness applied to the Adeptus Astartes, I adore how ridiculously bigger, stronger and faster the Custodes are. You feel that demigod might from the new models, sculpted with ornate markings and a cleanliness strange to see upon Imperium forces.

The Aquilon Terminator Sodality features five of the formidable Custodes in Aquilon Terminator armor, as if they weren't intimidating  enough. The Gyrfalcon Jetbike Sodality gives two of the galaxy's most overqualified janitors jetbikes armed with heavy guns. If that's not enough vehicular carnage, the Pallas Grav-Attacks are even faster and deadlier than the jetbikes. Finally, the biggest of them all is the Telemon Heavy Dreadnought, the apex of mechanical combat in its class.

Several classic Horus Heresy Custodes kits are also getting re-releases.

  • Shield-Captain
  • Custodian Guard Sodality
  • Sentinel Guard Sodality
  • Venatari Sodality
  • Custodian Dreadnought
  • Caladius Grav-Tank
  • Caladius Annihilator Grav-Tank
  • Coronus Grav-Carrier

For those looking to build up their golden company for Warhammer 40,000,  Combat Patrol: Adeptus Custodes is the way to go, and it includes:

  • 1x Shield-Captain
  • 6x Sentinel Guard
  • 3x Venatari
  • 1x Custodian Dreadnought

Alongside all these pretty models are the new rules for Adeptus Custodes in Warhammer 40k 11th edition. If you haven't  started your Custodes collection, then this week's the best chance to get started. You can read more details over at the Warhammer Community website.

Want to talk about those new rules for the God-Emperor's favorites? The Wargamer Discord is a great place for Warhammer 40k discussion.

title: MTG's oddest Secret Lair deck launches tomorrow
content:
Sometimes Magic: the Gathering Secret Lair drops contain a handful of cards, and sometimes Wizards of the Coast just decides to release an entire deck. Odds and Ends is a Commander deck that will be available to purchase from the Official MTG Secret Lair store from Monday, September 28th 9am Pacific Time to Tuesday, September 28th 9am Pacific Time.

Odds and Ends is a Commander deck all about playing cards with odd numbered mana values. It's led by Yennett, Cryptic Sovereign, a rare MTG card first printed in 2018. Yennett allows cards to be cast from the top of the library for free if they their cost is an odd number. This effect triggers whenever she damages an opponent. The deck features several cards illustrated by Ricardo Cavolo that look both otherworldly, yet also colorful and innocent. This is a deliberately unusual mixture, fitting the theme of oddness that the deck is striving for.

The decklist was officially revealed yesterday, although it had previously leaked back in August. Almost every single card that it contains has an odd mana value save for some Mana Rocks that cost two and also, for some reason, a copy of the four mana interstellar planeswalker Space Beleren.

In terms of reprints, the most notable card included in the deck is Esper Sentinel which, at the time of writing, is a roughly $60 (£45) card. It also features the $43 (£32)deck manipulating staple Sensei's Diving Top and the $20 (£15) even number hating Eldrazi Void Winnower.

Odds and Ends is being printed to demand, although only a limited number of copies will be shipped right away. Most customers will have their order fulfilled during the summer of 2027. The deck will be sold for $149 (£112).

Now I know what you're thinking. When are the even numbers going to get their turn? Well worry not, since you can build one right now by using Gyruda, Doom of Depths as either your Commander or a companion. What are some of the oddest deck themes that you've ever tested out? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord server.

title: This violently gothic TTRPG makes DnD campaigns look wholesome
content:
Dungeons and Dragons is a game so old that it has welcomed every kind of setting under the sun, and that includes Dark Sun. From the pulpy sci-fi of Eberron to whatever the heck is going on in Planescape, DnD does have quite a few worlds of darkness. That said, the bulk of most games will be set in the Forgotten Realms, a setting of mostly good ol' fashioned adventuring fun.

This upcoming TTRPG is good ol' fashioned gothic misery.

Fragged Aeternum 2 by Wade Dyer is a dark gothic fantasy TTRPG where players fight and die in the city of Aeternum's endless violence.  On the bright side, you are immortal. Unfortunately, everyone else is very curious how immortal you really are. The setting certainly wouldn't feel out of place for Warhammer 40k factions given the sheer amount of violence you'll encounter in an average campaign.

The game runs on the Fragged system, which ambitiously attempts to accommodate all styles of play. Whether you're a roleplay theater kid or power gaming fiend, Fragged will ensure you can play in the same game with different kinds of people. Besides, nothing brings players together than failing over and over again. The mechanics and narrative of Fragged Aeternum is best summed up by its tagline:

"After ten thousand thousand generations have each walked ten billion billion years towards the horizon, they shall stand no closer to the city's edge then whence they began." 

Seriously, that's the type of line that wouldn't be out of place in the Warhammer 40k games.

What I love most about Fragged Aeternum 2 is how it weaves the narrative and mechanics into the player's immortality.  Consequences come not from death, but genuine failure. If you let the big bad kill you in the final battle, you may wake underneath a mountain of corpses, each a life you failed to save.  It gives a deliciously dark edge to what could easily feel like a power fantasy.

You can support Fragged Aeternum 2 on Kickstarter.

title: This "reverse heist" board game punishes the loot hoarder in you
content:
Board games still have so much fun fantasy shenanigans, even without the roleplay elements in focus. I've always been tickled by roleplaying in board games that don't even have mechanics for it. Especially when you encounter those games with such a hilariously TTRPG premise that you just can't help but play along.

Such as dealing with a very grumpy dragon bereft of their belongings.

The Unheist of Heartburn House by Zero Strategy Games is a board game of competitive casual chaos as players take on the role of kobolds way in over their heads. They must run around returning the "borrowed" goods from Heartburn House, avoiding the dragon's wrath all the while. Of the DnD races, Kobolds are famously among the most diminutive, and these ones don't even have the benefit of high-level spells.

It's simply good game design to have players going for each other's throats. Nothing is funnier than seeing a player go wild with returning loot, only to be pushed into the path of an errant dragon breath. It really captures the vibe of those chaotic DnD sessions that everyone is canonically fated to have. Except this time, your DnD classes won't save you with abilities. All you've got are fast lil' feet and slightly less lil' brains.

The game takes place on a revolving board, keeping the house's layout in constant flux. Players must return to loot the best spots for even higher points. The player with the most points by the end wins the game, but that doesn't mean you can't make temporary alliances. Then again, it might be better to just screw everyone else over in repentance to the dragon overlord. Ultimately, the goal is to have fun and not die of premature combustion.

title: The solo TTRPG about surviving an office of dinosaurs is prehysterical
content:
Office work tends to be among the reasons why people throw themselves into the hobby of tabletop RPGs. Even in the most passionate of career paths, there's a certain drudgery on off days that make TTRPGs so enticing. Still, there should be something for those who do love the office and just want a bit more spice beside the water cooler.

And nothing's spicier than dinosaurs.

Dinosaur Office by wyrmturn is a solo journaling RPG where you finish a typical nine-to-five shift, doing all the things that Office Joes, Janes and Jhey/Jhems do. There's just one catch: every single one of your co-workers are dinosaurs. From Kent the Kentrosaurus to Fuki the Fukuiraptor, these loveable dinos are quite entertaining. So long as they think you're a fellow dino.  Sure, some of the more fantastical DnD races may stand a chance against these dinosaurs, a base human absolutely doesn't.

The game requires a standard deck of playing cards, a six-sided die, and your trusty journal. A club or spade card is an office task,  be that fixing the broken copier or finding whoever stole your stapler. With your luck in this universe, the stapler's probably trapped in amber instead of jelly. The heart and diamond cards represent a dinosaur task, such as clawing open packages or planning a communal tar pit.

A d6 roll will then decide the outcome of these tasks, six being most successful and one very much not. Your chances of surviving a fail are about as good as an Imperial Guardsman in Warhammer 40k 11th edition. The RPG reminds me of fellow one-pager Honey Heist, where much of the comedy comes from the premise and the players' imagination. These game jams are as satisfying as a fossil hunt for finding hidden gems.

You can check out Dinosaur Office for free on itch.io.

title: The next Pokémon TCG expansion features the most hauntingly beautiful illustration of a sea urchin that I've ever seen
content:
Every Pokémon out there is someone's favorite, and thanks to Pokémon TCG artist Tetsu Kayama, Pincurchin, the sea urchin Pokémon, is sure to gain a few more fans. When the Delta Reign expansion launches in November, the unusual echinoderm will appear on an illustration rare card that shows off the unnerving elegance of the deep sea.

Someone at the Pokémon Company clearly likes Pincurchin. After debuting in Pokémon Sword and Shield in 2019, Pincurchin has appeared in the game 9 times, sometimes on quite Rare Pokémon cards. There was a Pincurchin ex in Ascended Heroes, an alternative color shiny variant in Shining Fates, and now there's an illustration rare copy in Delta Reign.

The IR Pincurchin was officially revealed in an NME article earlier this week. The artwork depicts a group of Pincurchins clustered together around an underwater rock formation. There's a beam of light shining in from the bottom left, perhaps representing the flash of a camera, or the glow emanating from a submersible. This light gradually grows weaker and fades out, dimming almost completely by the time you reach the top right edge of the artwork. This use of light conveys the idea that the viewer is descending into an unwelcoming, but beautiful, alien world.

In terms of gameplay, Pincurchin's card doesn't quite do its artwork justice. As an 80hp basic Pokémon, with nothing to evolve into, it's pretty frail. Its Energy Crush attack deals 20 damage for every energy card attached to all of your opponent's Pokémon. While this has the potential to dish out lots of damage, Pincurchin almost certainly won't survive whatever counterattack your opponent cooks up on their next turn.

We definitely need more Pokémon cards depicting deep sea scenes. Perhaps an illustration rare Chinchou that captures the incredible strangeness of an anglerfish, or a Kyogre card showing the legendary water type flanked by all of the denizens of the deep. title: Explore a new Warhammer 40k-style galaxy in this grimdark TTRPG
content:
Warhammer 40,000 sits atop the throne of grimdark sci-fi fantasy, and with good (or in humanity's case, really bad) reason. Games Workshop has then expanded that galaxy over the decades, solidifying its vice grip on the fandom. Still, plenty of upstarts are looking to ruin the lives of their very own galaxies. Of those newcomers, this upcoming TTRPG looked very promising.

YATAGAN RPG is an upcoming dark sci-fi tabletop RPG set in a cosmos of eternal conflict.  Gods and men alike crash into each other with steel and starships in a setting where you are free to rise and fall in glorious violence.  Instead of the wargaming rules of Warhammer 40k 11th edition, Yatagan is a TTRPG system based around colored d12, each color tied to elements of the game and its many denizens.

Yatagan welcomes players into its universe with its very first setting: the Nomad Worlds. Heavily inspired by Turkic mythology, the setting has three major factions. Ulgen, the Radiant One reigns supreme upon the Solemn Orbs, claiming themselves champions of light and order. Erlik the Hollow One rules over the Umbral Ring, the edge of the known universe filled with death and chaos.

Against these two factions stands alone Gesar the Nomad, leader of the Emerald Horde and eager to throw the gods off their thrones and free the galaxy from their celestial grip. Just as the Warhammer 40k factions do, these groups all hate each other with a burning passion. But this being a TTRPG, you should be concerned about yourself first and foremost.

The character creation of Yatagan is what drew me most mechanically. Entirely classless, the system revolves around Birthright and Edges. A Birthright defines your starting wealth, skills, abilities and equipment. Edges, meanwhile, are akin to feats from DnD, which you can acquire throughout your adventures. This makes Yatagan a very dynamic TTRPG, unrestrained by the linearity of a traditional class system.

For more on the rules, you can follow YATAGAN RPG on Backerkit and receive a free copy of the quickstart.

title: These DnD-style death game adventures are 95% off on Fanatical
content:
Dungeons and Dragons is obviously an entertaining game, and it's just as fun to watch others play it. There's a 99% chance the person reading this has watched a bit of Critical Role or Dimension 20 at some point. However, for those who want a bit more sudden death in their entertainment, stories such as Dungeon Crawler Carl tend to be where they gravitate. If you've ever wanted to experience being a Carl, look no further than this bundle.

The Xcrawl RPG Bundle features 40 books from the Xcrawl series for only $18 USD, a massive discount from their combined retail price of $339 USD. Xcrawl is a spin-off of the beloved Dungeon Crawl Classics line, a system inspired by old-school DnD, with all of its esoteric theming and brutal difficulty. That ramps up even further in Xcrawl Classics, as superstar athletes of various DnD classes compete in the death sport of competitive dungeon crawling.

If you're at all a fan of Dungeon Crawler Carl, The Running Man, Mojo World from the X-Men stories, and finally, pro wrestling, then Xcrawl classics is an absolute must-get. It's hard to describe this series as anything else but chaotic and loud. Expect these sessions to be a death clown circus, as players are quite literally performing for the live audience of the North American empire.

I love seeing how DnD races adapt to this futuristic setting. It tickles me to see dragons and goblins televised, it's like seeing a childhood friend holding a lightsaber. One of my favorite smaller adventures that really capture that vibe is Tropicrawl Cataclysm, an event set in Miami where gatormen on rocket-powered jetskis try to lop your head off with axes. If that doesn't sell you on the premise, then there's about 39 other wacky adventures for you to suit your fancy.

You can grab the Xcrawl RPG Bundle on Fanatical until November 17, 2026.

title: [40k] Breaking Down LGT: Factions, Dispositions, & More
content:
Over the last few years, the London Grand Tournament (LGT) has slowly taken the crown for being the largest singles event in the world for Warhammer 40k with 1,028 registered players coming into this weekend. With that in mind, we decided to take a look at this weekend's lists and breaking down the current meta before everything is thrown into upheaval by the upcoming Codex: Space Marines update next week.

Faction Break Down

Cedit to date from Listforge.info

LGT has been able to scrounge together at least one player for every single faction, something that many events can’t manage. Usually at best a large event will have a single lone weirdo bucking the trend defiantly with Imperial Agents, demanding they be taken seriously (Editor: No). LGT has a whopping six, beating out its count of Deathwatch players - four (Editor: Wrap it up, Deathwailures).

At the top of the meta Orks and Custodes mark the top spots by volume, followed by Marines and Dark Angels. Fun Fact: There are almost as many Allarus Terminators in lists as attendees, with 870 of the dumb golden terminators (this is according to one of my friends, don't blame me if that math is wrong). These are the big meta threats; all of them either barely got nerfed in the last slate, or recently received a crazy powerful codex to shoot them to the top (Orks).

After the top four there are a few surprises: Necrons, Emperor's Children, Chaos Space Marines, and Tyranids make up the next four top factions by volume. Necrons generally are very popular in the UK, and have been consistently good since the start of 10th edition, so I am not shocked to see them here; same with Emperor's Children, who still are doing okay even after their big nerfs. Chaos Space Marines are a bit more unique; they have done fine in 11th edition so far haven't been dominant since Defilers and three quarters of the units supporting them received multiple points hikes. That said, they've always been a popular faction, and that'll be a factor here. Same kind of goes for Tyranids, who tend to be disappointing in 11th edition even with Norns, but gained a huge popularity boost from showing up in the 10th edition starter box.

T’au and Votann round out the top ten factions and are where we drop below the 5% threshold per faction. These are both okay factions; neither is considered too overpowered or bad, and both are likely driven a bit by a mix of solid faction performance and faction specialization. Then we have most of the other decent factions, with a few stand-outs like World Eaters and Grey Knights having much higher faction percentages then their win rate would suggest they deserve.

Rounding out the bottom five, Chaos Knights barely beat out Adepta Sorotiats for number six by just one player. We have Adepta Soroitas with eighteen players, Black Templars with fourteen, GSC with eight, Imperial Agents with six, and Deathwatch with four. Two of these lower player count armies are Space Marines which is often expected due to other Space Marine chapters that are more powerful dragging away all but the most dedicated players. The other three are all examples of factions that just have not quite hit the mark in 11th and are again most likely just drawing on the most dedicated faction specialists.

Now that we understand the armies of LGT, let's break down the next most important part of 11th: Army Dispositions.

Dispositions

Credit for data from Listforge.info

At first glance, this looks pretty bad for balance. On a deeper dive, it looks even worse - Take and Hold and Priority Assets take up a combined 62% of lists at the event, which in a world where there are three total options that would be perfect. Unfortunately, we live in the world with five options, and that's not a great outlook for the Disposition meta.

Take and Hold and Priority Assets are both the go-to disposition options for the field, they are both very similar to how 10th played: Hold objectives and maybe do an action. That's very easy for pretty much any army no matter how it is built, it's just a question of whether you need action goobers. In regard to Priority Assets, in a world where there are only two action secondaries - both of which give a free redraw when held together - it is really easy to plan on doing your mission action without having to worry too much about action economy.

Reconnaissance and Purge the Foe both can require a bit more to run, but for two different reasons. Most armies are totally fine running Purge the Foe, but it is very hard to pick as most of the best detachments lost easy access to Purge the Foe in the balance dataslate a few months ago, while the ones who do still have it tend to be on the lower power level. Reconnaissance is a bit odd in that a few of its missions are a bit closer to Take and Hold then to a recon-style mission, meaning your army has to both be able to spread across the board, while also being able to run a traditional hold primary style, which can be a challenge. This is offset in part by the Darkflight Pursuit Detachment, which just makes up for it by tabling opponents quickly.

The final option, Disruption with a measly forty five champions, is a travesty. You basically only run Disruption if you are forced to, or if you are the best player in the world having a laugh. This primary has to do so much more work for way fewer points in comparison to the rest of the field and often feels like playing with a handicap.

The Top Players

Now that we have broken down the field, let's take a look at some of the heavy hitters to watch going into this weekend. While we all know what to expect from Custodes, Dark Angels, and Orks, let's look at a few lists that break the model and their players.

I think this event breakdown really puts into focus how polarized the current meta is. It's been a week since we began our exhaustive coverage of Codex: Space Marines for 11th Edition, a big linktree for which you can find here (and replicated a little bit down this very page). There was a lot of big news coming out of the changes in that book, especially the ones made to Lion El'Jonson -- and then there was even more news on Monday, with more changes still, shifting the points on the Lion. We covered all of that in our first 40K Weekend Update:

  • 40K Weekend Update: The Lion Takes a Points Hike, Orks Bully Events

You might also notice the other half of that headline -- we're not long on the heels of Codex: Orks, and that book was quite strong, doing very well in competitive events as its rules became table-legal. You can find more about the specific rules interactions new to that army in our Ruleshammer column on the subject as well as advice on how to play against the green menace in the subscriber-only section of our website ($), authored by competitive player Isaac Terada. This article isn't about Orks, though. In addition to the Weekend Update, we began another feature in front of the paywall for players looking to take Space Marines to the table and maybe win a few games:

  • Lore to Table: Building Imperial Fists with the 11th Edition Codex

The Lore to Table series will begin with a focus on Space Marine and Space Marine-adjacent Chapters and factions; look for another entry into the series concerning the Lion himself next week. Speaking of lore-accurate Space Marine armies on the table, we've also begun updating our How to Paint Everything Space Marine articles from editions past; two of those ran this week:

  • How To Paint Everything: Space Wolves Space Marines (Updated September 23, 2026)
  • How to Paint Everything: Ultramarines Space Marines (Updated September 25, 2026)

More of those are on the way as well, thanks to master painter Keewa. If you're going to be doing some painting, there are some new paints on the way that you might want to consider, and Rob and Rich got their hands on them as well:

  • Tabletop Battles Reviews: Warhammer Tone Pro Paints

For our subscribers, we've a got a lot more Space Marine-focused list and meta play content coming in the pipeline as our pros get more time to fool around with the new points and rules on the table, but to start you off, Innes Wilson gave a broad overview of how he sees unit roles broadly changing across the new Space Marines Codex earlier this week:

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Warhammer Tone Pro Paints
content:
Games Workshop's new line of Warhammer Tone Pro paints have been announced, promising great coverage, intense colours, and usability across different application methods. They are also presented in pentads, with each set of five paints sharing a name, and receiving a number from 1 (dark) to 5 (light). Rob and Rich have had some hands on time with the paints, ready to share their initial thoughts.

We'd like to thank Games Workshop for providing us with a preview set of these paints for review purposes.

TheChirurgeon: A set of these dropped on my door Wednesday night, giving me a selection of the new paints. Specifically, there was a full set of Blue paints, i.e. #1-5 for Blue Gorkshroom, a trio of Reds (Bloodtoof Red), a trio of greens (Hierotek Green), Black/Grey/White, and one each of Pink, Orange, Yellow, and Bright Green. That's a pretty solid set, though it did leave me wanting more pinks and yellows to play with - my specific interest in these is what their coverage looks like for light colors over black primer, because priming white is for cowards.

There were some issues with the paints, but these struck me as more QC issues than issues with the paints themselves. Specifically, in both of the sets I opened, one or more of the pots was leaking. It didn't seem like they were properly sealed, leading to paint dripping out and/or separating.

Loading...

I opened two different boxes of these - the preview set I was sent by Games Workshop and a second box at my local Warhammer store - and both had this issue. Like I said, I don't think it's a problem with the paints themselves but more how they're packaged - it seemed like the lids either weren't on completely or weren't closed. That said, the boxes we were sent are notably not going to be sold on shelves, and are more just sampler packs for demos, so the final product may have better quality control.

What About That Coverage, Though?

My big immediate reaction on seeing these paints was "I want to try the pinks to do Emperor's Children." And that was my immediate first go-to here, testing the paint on a pair of Emperor's Children models which I had already primed black. Painting the pink on these is usually a very involved process, starting with multiple thin coats of Pink Horror and working my way up to Emperor's Children. If I can replace that with a single step of pink, or just two and some shading, I'm in.

Loading...

There are basically four things I'm really testing when it comes to these paints:

  1. How's their coverage? This was advertised as excellent, so I want to know how good it is. I want to test lights over darks, and black over everything.
  2. How does it handle being "gooped on" to the model? This is another area where early reviews and preview video have suggested it'll look great.
  3. How does it blend? Can I mix it with other Tone Pro colors and how smooth are the transitions when I layer them up?
  4. How will it look when I start using other paints, especially my older paints?

One key thing about these paints is that they seem to be alcohol-based, and so will not mix with the water-based paints of the standard Citadel range.. They tend to dry pretty rapidly still - even goopy I was looking at about 15 minutes for them to dry - and they tended to produce a nice finish, though I think you'll still want to use your brush to avoid leaving obvious brush marks or streaks.

Loading...

Coverage on the pink was generally very good. I really felt it needed to coats to get there, but the coats could go on pretty thick and resolved nicely into something that didn't lose detail. They were also incredibly vibrant - the pink is much brighter and pinker than the pink I painted over black with my other models using Pink Horror and Emperor's Children. After I laid down those coats, I ended up using Carroburg Crimson to shade the edges and glaze coats of Emperor's Children to blend up to a lighter pink before using Fulgrim Pink to do my edge highlighting and the filigree work.

You can see the difference in saturation: The Tone Pro model is on the left; the older, Pink Horror/EC model is on the right. I'm really happy with how the model turned out and while it's a bit pinker than my older models, I'm OK to keep using this moving forward.

Loading...

After pink came yellow. My best opportunity for doing yellow testing right now is hazard stripes on Iron Warriors so I picked up one of my Mutilators and used him as a test model, painting one coat of Khemri Sands (4) over the black primer. I'd later correct with Blackstone Void (1), which I gotta tell you - it's an amazing black. I previously used Black Legion Contrast paint for doing base rims; I can tell you right now that I will never do that again - Blackstone Void is now the black baserim color of choice. It's just really smooth, covers well, and tends to smooth out brushstrokes as it dries, which is amazing.

Loading...

I tested the reds on some Red Corsairs models, using all three tones for highlights and I was impressed with how they seem to self-blend into lower number colors. Normally I do some semi-complicated wet blending with my reds for Red Corsairs armor panels but this time just layering on 2-3-4 of Bloodtoof Red worked remarkably well. I finished it off with Carroburg recesses and Wild Rider Red highlights, but Ideally I can do both of those with Tone Pro paints in the future.

Then there was the white. I don't paint a lot of models white these days but I'll say that the Tone Pro White (Blackstone Void 5) did a fantastic job covering over black. You'd still want two coats - I only used one above - but I'd easily place it on par with my Monument Hobbies white paint or Reaper's Pure White.

I went back and did a second coat of white (Blackstone Void 5) on the Death Guard model I originally put a coat on, and I was pretty confident that I could do two coats to get a full white over black if I wanted to on future models. It's really solid.

Cronch: I'm really intrigued by these paints, and jumped at the opportunity to try them out. Given Rob's efforts above, I decided to focus on two main areas. First, I'd use the full range of Blue Gorkshroom 1-5 to paint something, choosing a nice flat area to cover smooth basecoating, glazing, and edge highlighting. Secondly, I'd try out some of the other common techniques on another piece - airbrushing, washing, and drybrushing.

Tone Pro test subjects. Credit: Rich Nutter

For my flat panel, I chose the missile launcher arm of a Ballistus Dreadnought, which I'd handily built earlier this week. I primed it up in Colour Forge Standard Grey spray, then set to work. My goal here was to be able to both shade down and highlight up, so I based the panel in Blue Gorkshroom 3. The paint was thinner than I was expecting, but I thought it covered surprisingly well given this. I did thin it down a little on a wet palette, but not much. The size of the flat areas on the arm did mean I needed to do roughly 4 thin coats, and compared to several other examples of Tone Pro's shrinking and self-leveling properties I was a little disappointed here. Although the paint did dry quickly and smoothly, I felt that if an area was too wet it was still quite likely to leave tide marks behind as it dried. I expect this would be less likely on something more organically shaped though, and I was able to smooth it out with subsequent coats.

Basecoat: Blue Gorkshroom 3. Credit: Rich Nutter

Following the basecoat, I glazed some shadows towards the top of each panel, first with Blue Gorkshroom 2 then subsequently with Blue Gorkshroom 1, thinning the paint with water and applying in thin coats. The paint thinned down well with water on the palette, with colour still seeming pretty saturated in the mix and no issues with splitting whilst sat. I did find once again that I was getting some tide marks, although I do have an important caveat, in that I was doing this with limited time and trying to work faster than I normally would. In all likelihood, my coats weren't as thin nor my brush as empty as they really needed to be. I'd be interested to retry this using the two different Tone Pro mediums and see if that made a difference.

Glaze shade: Blue Gorkshroom 2. Credit: Rich Nutter

Glaze shade: Blue Gorkshroom 1. Credit: Rich Nutter

After shading I tidied up with Blue Gorkshroom 3, before highlighting some edges with 4 and 5. I also added some scratches with 5, which I reinforced with Blackstone Void 1. I felt that the paint applied well here, thinning well for highlights and staying workable on the brush for a decent length of time. Despite the paint's relative thinness out of the pot (sidenote: I did knock a pot over, and wow I spilled a lot of it in the time it took to catch) it didn't flow off the brush too fast to be controllable, and it also retained a strong colour, saving the need to reinforce the highlights multiple times.

Edge highlight: Blue Gorkshroom 4. Credit: Rich Nutter

Spot highlight: Blue Gorkshroom 5. Credit: Rich Nutter

I was left with one issue at the end, which is that these paints are really quite a shiny satin, a fact which I think was exacerbating my issues with the tide marks of the glaze step. As an experiment, I opted to hit the piece with an ultra-matte varnish, and I think that does show off the results a bit better. I don't think it's a necessity, of course, as you may prefer a different finish on your models!

After ultra-matte varnish. Credit: Rich Nutter

Rob: Damn, that looks great.

Cronch: I decided to stick with Blue Gorkshroom for some more testing, so I dug out a Space Marine Librarian from Armageddon, already primed in Colour Forge Bestiary Brown. I basecoated through the airbrush with Blue Gorkshroom 1, before doing some rough zenithal with 2 and 3. I thinned the paint somewhere between 1:1 and 2:1 thinner:paint, using regular Vallejo Airbrush Thinner. I was really impressed with how these airbrush! I had a solid coat in roughly 2 passes, and the colour intensity was really notable. The paint dried well, and stayed smooth.

Basecoat: Blue Gorkshroom 1. Credit: Rich Nutter

Zenithal: Blue Gorkshroom 2. Credit: Rich Nutter

Zenithal: Blue Gorkshroom 3. Credit: Rich Nutter

I figured it was worth trying out the Tone Pro Shading Medium too, so I mixed down some Blackstone Void 1 with roughly 5 brushes of medium per brush of paint, and then washed it all over the model. The wash seemed pretty good at finding the recesses whilst avoiding unsightly pooling, and I'd say it stained the same or slightly less than current Nuln Oil - that is, it did change the surface colour, but not too much. It mixed well, and I can see this being a great tool for mixing washes of light colours to fill in glowing eyes, plasma weapons and the like.

Wash: 5:1 Shading Medium:Blackstone Void 1. Credit: Rich Nutter

Once the wash was dry, it was time to try out some drybrushing! Using a soft, round Artis Opus drybrush, I built up a coat of Blue Gorkshroom 3 to re-establish the colour, before moving on to 4 and 5 to catch the edges and define the model. The paints drybrushed pretty well, I wouldn't say it felt like anything revolutionary but the saturated colours combined with the thinner paint did feel a little like it wasn't clogging up the brush as much. It's certainly a viable technique though, and it's always nice to have more ways to use your paints.

Drybrush: Blue Gorkshroom 3. Credit: Rich Nutter

Drybrush: Blue Gorkshroom 5. Credit: Rich Nutter

Drybrush: Blue Gorkshroom 4. Credit: Rich Nutter

Just as an aside, I know it's a bit odd to go to the effort of airbrushing some volumes just to wash and drybrush over them! Primarily, I wanted to test the different methods in a limited amount of time, and for an actual project I think you'd be able to get a good result with any mix of methods.

Finally, I decided to do a quick coverage tester on some brighter colours.

Tone Pro bright colours test. Credit: Rich Nutter

Left to right, that's Hierotek Green 3 (two coats), Chotec Orange 4 (three coats), Plague Toad Venom 5 (three coats), and the confusingly-named Blackstone Void 5 (two coats). I'm impressed with the coverage on all of these, especially the white which made me exclaim out loud as I applied the first coat. The orange is a good match for Troll Slayer Orange, and the green for Warpstone Glow. That's a pair of paints with pretty diabolical coverage, so these could easily find a place as more reliable replacements. Overall, the coverage hasn't come at the cost of detail - these were all applied with a decently sized flat brush, straight from the pot, and there's no significant obscuring of detail. My apologies to these Uruk Hai Scouts, who are now thoroughly the wrong colours for a life in Middle-Earth.

Final Thoughts

TheChirurgeon: These are an absolute departure from the standard paints Games Workshop puts out, and I'm very impressed with them. It took me a long time to become comfortable with Contrast paints - I think they're actually pretty bad for what they're advertised as - and using them for specific effects really changed how I felt about them. These on the other hand, have more or less convinced me out of the box. I'm not planning to toss my existing paints, but I'm definitely interested in picking up specific sets of these and planning armies around them. I don't know that this is how I'll be doing all of my Emperor's Children from now on - I need to color match new models to the ones I've already done - but the next army or two is likely to be one I paint using these for the base coats.

Cronch: It's been quite a while since we've seen any real innovation from Games Workshop when it comes to paint ranges, and these do appear to be a genuinely different offering. Time will tell as to whether they become an integral part of a painter's toolbox, but I am quite taken with the saturated colours and the thinner consistency. I'm really looking forward to trying more of the pink range, as I've been impressed with how well the brighter colours cover. I'm looking forward to hearing more peoples' thoughts as we see the full range released!

title: Black Library Readers’ Hall of Fame: The Winners of 2017, and Class of 2018
content:
The Black Library Readers’ Hall of Fame is Tabletop Battles’s long-term, reader-participation initiative to recognize those novels that have “cultural, historical, or aesthetic significance” to the Black Library. Through the votes of readers as well as our community panel of community voices, we’ll examine the entire history of the Black Library, induct the latest winners, and vote for the next round’s candidates every other week.

We're now just under a decade out from modern day, and many of the novels we're looking at will begin to be more familiar to many readers who have come into the hobby in the last few years. Dark Imperium is still on many bookstore shelves, The Devastation of Baal was a recent hardcover reissue, and Red Tithe was only last year brought back in a Special Edition.

The past is increasingly present.

2017 was another highlight year for the Black Library as well, with nine books being voted into the Black Library Readers' Hall of Fame!

As a reminder, if you're really enjoying this project and want to see it from a different angle, the companion piece, The Hall Monitor, runs over at my Substack, The Warhammer Wordforge. A cross between a director's commentary and behind-the-scenes look, each installment we dive a little deeper into a particular element of the Readers' Hall of Fame project. Hope to see you there!

The Envelope Please

Now, let's get to the stars of the show, the books inducted for 2017!

Michael, Track of Words: "Darkly fascinating and beautifully crafted, with a deceptively simple plot providing immense scope for character development. It’s also, as you might expect from Dembski-Bowden, remarkably lore-heavy…but in a very good way, adding detail and depth to the characters and story without ever dominating."

Michael, Track of Words: "On the surface this is a simple story of inquisitors hunting bad guys, but over the course of the book – and, without spoiling anything, some of the most interesting ideas are reserved for the later stages – things gradually become bigger, more dangerous and more unexpectedly interesting. Wraight keeps us guessing throughout, slowly unveiling more players and their motivations, while hinting at so much more going on behind the scenes. Wraight’s writing, storytelling and plotting are all as good as you’d expect here"

Michael, Track of Words: "Haley managed to somehow combine elements of earlier stories, a nuanced and powerful character study, an incredibly vivid depiction of Baal and the Blood Angels, and an effective lead-in to what’s coming next, all in a single coherent piece…it’s a truly impressive achievement. This redefined 40k-era Blood Angels from the top down, expanding their culture and customs beyond anything we’ve seen before. Outstanding."

Gus, Black Library Subreddit: "Dark Imperium is another home run by Haley. His novels were given the task of telling pivotal tales of the new era of the imperium, in this case the return of the First Primarch in nine thousand years or so. Here he is consistently good, his stories are great at balancing character development and grand scale action, and he is great at telling epic tales with several threads that he brings home in satisfying fashion.

"The novel does an excellent job in showing us Guilliman’s POV as he learns about the current state of the imperium and how it has done a 180-degree turn from the time he last saw it. This is also why it is a great entry point novel for newcomers, because the primarch reborn himself feels like a stranger in his old home. Just like he did with Dante Haley shows us the humanity of these larger-than-life characters and why we should care about them."

Gus, Black Library Subreddit: "Devastation of Baal is a must-read for the post rift timeline. And thankfully Guy Haley knocked it out of the park. It is kind of a sequel to Haley’s Dante, but the focus is obviously wider as we set foot in the Blood Angels’ home world and witness the despair from the consequences of the Fall of Cadia reaching across the galaxy. This is an epic novel full of lore drops and just brutal and unapologetic action. Haley really brings home the notion of the imperium being beset on all sides, including the threats from within as the Blood Angels must deal with their genetic curses on top of the Tyranid invasion."

Michael, Track of Words: "Make no mistake, this is a big story, not just in context of the Blood Angels but the whole 40k setting. That crossover between old and new 40k is cleverly woven into the story and doesn’t take away from the power of the main narrative, but just adds an extra burst of excitement. As both the culmination of a major 40k storyline of the time and the start of a major new series (Space Marine Conquests), this delivered in spades."

Michael, Track of Words: "Beautifully done, each character has a distinct voice that sets them apart from the others and there’s a great balance between the characters, and between the political intrigue of Terra and the actions of two of the most powerful fighting forces in the Imperium. That balance – between politics and action – is perhaps the most important element to the book, and where it really shines. An absolute must-read."

Michael, Track of Words: "A fascinating book, which doesn’t suffer in the slightest for a decreased focus on action compared to many Black Library titles. It’s also pretty dark, as for all that he’s an engaging character with a strangely paternal attitude to a lot of his creations, he’s still fairly monstrous. Or as Reynolds himself put it, 'I wanted to use Clonelord to remind readers that he’s still kind of a piece of crap.'"

Michael, Track of Words: "As a novel tasked with not just providing an entertaining story but also detailing what will be a brand new chapter to a lot of readers, there’s a lot to cover here – but MacNiven pulls it off with aplomb. He carefully rations the hints and teasers about the Carcharadons’ past and background in order to add interest without revealing too much, and likewise doesn’t overplay the Polynesian influences or shark references in order to add depth and character without straying into caricature.

"Going with Night Lords as antagonists proves a fantastic choice, allowing for opportunities to really emphasise the core darkness of 40k, and both tonally and structurally it feels like an old-school dark 40k novel updated for the more modern tastes of Black Library readers."

Jay, Tabletop Battles and Warhammer Wordforge: "Typically by the time you get this deep in a long-running series, you're not expecting to see a lot of Hall consideration. After all, the books typically rely heavily on the ones that came before and tend to be viewed through the lens of the overall series rather than as a standalone book. But as we've seen before, Abnett has shown an uncanny ability to continue to reinvent this franchise and with The Warmaster, Colonel-Commissar Ibram Gaunt steps into the shoes of a Lord Generalship. It's fantastic military worldbuilding, and the story's mix of planet-level strategy with the struggles of the individual Ghosts is more than enough to see it win reader support for induction."

Congratulations to all the worthy winners!

The Ballot: The Class of 2018

As noted previously, the polling issues we're experiencing here on Tabletop Battles are ongoing, so going forward we'll be using Google Forms (open poll, no need to be logged into Google).

To view the class of 2018 and cast your votes, please click here.

The Banner of Glory

Finally, here are all of the current members of the Black Library Readers' Hall of Fame.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? title: Warhammer, Death Metal and the Midlands: An Interview with Ash Moore of Mutagenic Host
content:
The Lamb’s a nice little local boozer in Surbiton. Ash Moore, vocalist for Mutagenic Host, is in the beer garden setting up a table for Spearhead. Inside the pub a guy is plugging an acoustic guitar into some amps.

It’s sunny. Kids are running around. One of their dads comes up and asks what we’re playing. He tells us he plays Kill Team and a bit of 40K when he gets the chance. Ash enthusiastically tells him about two clubs he is part of nearby.

You should come. It’s kid friendly too.

By the time we sort out the cards, board and terrain for our game, there is already soft music drifting from inside the pub. Ash gestures towards the open window and the singer beyond it.

He’s got a good voice. You into folk?

Yeah. I’ve been listening to a lot of Bulgarian Wedding Music at the moment.

So, you’re eclectic like me. I love folk.

Well, last time I saw you, you were growling into a mic at the Black Heart in Camden. For those who don't know Bob Dylan from their Cannibal Corpse, do you want to just introduce the band for us?

Yeah, so Mutagenic Host is a five piece Death Metal band from London, but we're all from different parts. I'm from Birmingham and I do the vocals, organise the band and do our socials. I also write all the lyrics. 

Credit: Keiffer Passey

Jack Thompson, he's from LA, he's the guitarist and is one of two song writers. Then Dan Bulford, who's from London, also writes and produces a lot of the music. Our bassist is called Eddie Swales, he's from London. And then George Kinella-Pearn, he's the drummer and he's from the Midlands, like me. 

We formed just as Covid ended. I was just searching for a creative output. I just think that the pandemic had such a huge effect on people. It had such a huge effect on me. A lot of people were so angry during that time. A lot of people's loved ones died because of Tory ineptitude and cronyism and I don't think it gets talked about enough.  It's been pushed under the rug. People are so horrified by it that it's almost traumatic. That made me really angry. At the same time, like many others, I got back into Warhammer for the first time since I was a child. I think Covid was a real diving board moment for the hobby; lots of people inside, nothing to do but fear for their mortal coil, so little plastic toy soldiers was the antidote - and death metal. 

Priority? 

We roll off and Ash gets a four to my one. He deploys his Maggotkin of Nurgle: Bleak Host. Today I’ve opted for Flesh Eater Courts Carrion Retainers.

You’ve got a lot of movement in your list. That’s where Nurgle struggles.  We don’t get round the board much.

I begin deploying my force while Ash tells me me how the band got its start.

credit: Ash More Three of us at the time, me, Dan and George were part of the hardcore scene in London. So we would be going to hardcore shows all the time. Dan and I had a band together previously called Downward Spiral, which is more like a crowbar, a depressing melodic-hardcore band.

But I always wanted to really have a proper crack at doing a Death Metal band. 

So, I put it on a Facebook page. Does anybody want to start a band? And I met Jack Thompson. We just became best friends straight away. His song writing credibility is one of the things that's carried this band all the way through. But all the members of this band are multi-talented and just incredible people.

We all are really supportive of one another. All of our family knows each other. Our whole life really revolves around the band.

Ash chooses to go first, clumping most of his units together and moving slowly forward in a big unkillable (but slow) blob of pestilent flesh, but sending one of his Pusgoyle Blightlords to toe an objective.  Being a Nurgle player myself, I know how it goes; move stuff into the middle and wait to see if your opponent is foolish enough to charge.

Not wanting to get bogged down in the middle for the rest of the game, I send my Morbheg Knights to go deal with the lone Blightlord, which mercifully they kill in one round (which is rare), and then send my Varghulf Courtier and my Abhorrant Archregent to toe an objective each, nudging me into the lead at the end of round one.

credit: Saelfe

So we started with the Genotoxic Demo. The first song we wrote was called the March of Pestilence and that was a song about the marching of families whose loved ones had died during COVID, this was due to the failures of the Tories for the most part. I abhor incompetence and posturing. We got on Dry Cough Records, which is the home of underground British Death Metal, and put out a tape. Tapes are synonymous with death metal, for a long time this is how the genre travelled by swapping tapes. It's a rite of passage for any self-respecting death metal band to put out a tape. We had a really good response and that spurred us on to make haste. 

Dry Cough Records sounds like the perfect record label for a Nurgle band!

We loved that label. We've moved away from it now, but we'll always have a place in our heart for it. Mutagenic Host is a Nurgle band. The name alone should conjure up visions of the Grandfathers Blessings. We have songs like ‘Metaphysical Maladies’ which is taken from a spell from the Malignant Spellcaster from Death Guard, or lyrics that include ‘rancid visitations’ which is a spell from Maggotkin in 3rd edition AOS. I own nearly 11k points of Nurgle Warhammer. Im missing Tarmukhan and his horde, Ignatius Grulgor who is the death guard Forge World Daemon Prince, Scabeiathrax the Bloated which is a Forge World Great Unclean one and Cor'bax Utterblight from the Horus Heresy. So I'm not missing a lot at all! If anyone is reading this and wants to part with any of those, let me know and make me the jolliest Nurglite on the planet, that would be kind. 

Tell me about the band name. Mutagenic Host is a pretty memorable name.

It’s all tied to bio-weaponry, eugenics - and Warhammer. A host can be the carrier of the mutagens, or host can also mean an army. Everything that I write has a dual meaning. 

Talking of mutagenic hosts, Ash wins priority into round two and moves his host of rotting fanatics closer to the central objective, not quite having the movement to dominate it, but certainly having enough to get a good number of Plaguebearer feet on it and make me think twice about trying to take it. He has enough battle tactic cards to get a decent score without having to take objectives off me.

You and I played AOS ages ago, maybe even the first time we met, and you told me then that you were in a band. I politely nodded and then forgot all about it. Then a year later I read this article about the revival of Death Metal in the UK, and it mentioned Mutagenic Host. I went and had a listen and messaged you right away saying something like, ‘you never told me you were in a GOOD band!’

We just seem to be getting better and better. It’s a beautiful thing. It’s a creative endeavour that I take incredibly seriously. In a world of throwaway garbage, popular figureheads who do more damage to the earth than good, and insidious overlords that are trying to infiltrate the way you think; to have a vehicle to try and disrupt that is incredibly important. 

We had a really great response early on. Even some of the opening shows that we were playing with all top quality death metal bands. Our first show was with Vacuous who are on Relapse Record, now. An incredible, incredible band. They gave us our first show. We also played with Incantation, who are just absolute legends. Then we played with another big band coming from the US called Undeath. So, you know, the quality of the demo allowed us to develop the band in a way that was professional and that felt that it was making a difference in the music scene. 

Credit: Kieffer Passey

And then you released The Diseased Machine. Which is just such an awesome album. 

We wrote Diseased Machine in about six months, maybe eight. The theme is the biggest talking point about that album, and I think it's why people resonate with it so much. It’s incredibly damning of AI and how the upper echelons of society have been so quick to allow Pandora’s Box to open without impunity; putting yours, mine, and the future of the children of this earth in complete jeopardy just because some play dough complexion nerd who got all his wealth from using children to mine minerals in Africa wants to act like a TEMU Tony Stark. Makes me fucking sick to the stomach.

I digress, the album tells the story of the destruction of humanity by AI. It’s actually the start of a trilogy of storytelling. Much like Warhammer, we create our own lore. It’s a lot of fun, if not taxing to some degree also. After the album we put out the Grotesque Union/ Chimeric Vestige 2026 promo, which is essentially about the last human organism left solitary on earth after the destruction of mankind, at the hands of the   machines that harvest human biomatter (sound familiar?) and their AI overlords. Then the next album we're doing is actually the prelude to all that.

It's science fiction. We're all massive 80s/90s film fans, Terminator, Videodrome, Soylent Green, you know, so all that kind of imagery comes into it. But the real takeaway from it is about the establishment around the world. I’m absolutely disgusted with how human life is so completely transient, left to rot, allowed to fester to meet their means. When you have children that are being bombed by drones in Gaza that utilise AI. And then you’ve got the likes of Palantir trying to take over the NHS, this oligarch of the wrong kind of nerds, is in itself, it’s a disease.

You know what I mean? Like, the complete disregard of human life is always so abhorrent to me and it's always so prevalent in all of this. All the actions of these demagogues who are always only out for their own end. It horrifies me. So it's easier to write an album that's about that than it is to go away and come up with the kind of imagery usually used in Death Metal songs. It's much easier to write about the horrors of the world than it is to actually fantasize about certain tropes in death metal. 

In my half of the dullest 2nd round of Spearhead ever played, I step just enough Cryptguard onto the objective to take control, and started to bring my Morbhegs and Varghulf Courtier back towards the centre for the inevitable bloodbath to come in round three, whilst making sure I score enough primary points and battle tactics to maintain a slim lead. 

Musically speaking, the album really has the feel of a classic 90s Death Metal record. There’s some serious groove to it.

Yeah, we always do groove. We never over produce. 

It was very stressful to record. We were all working our jobs and doing it on our own time. Once it was written we had to record it. That was really arduous. We went to one place, didn't work out, went to another place, didn't work out. We had to go and do vocals elsewhere. Then we ended up doing a lot of it at home where we would do it and then go and have it reamped to the studio. Thankfully there's a bloke called Boulty in Nottingham (Stuck on a Name Studios) Another Warhammer link! And he managed to put it all together.

And we don't give a shit what anybody thinks about us. A lot of bands say that, but we truly mean it. I think it comes off in the music.

We'll never put out music that we think will bore people. I mean, we're all very talented people, but it's never about technicality. It's always about feeling and it's always about groove, and it's always about how it relates back to people. And I think that's so much more important than being great musicians. Someone called us hooligan death metal once!

Ash wins priority and brings down his second Pusgoyle Blightlord and Plaguebearer units, using the Plaguebearers to steal an objective and charging his Blightlord, along with everything else, into my units at the centre of the board, embroiling my Vargulf and Cryptguard in the fray. He decimates the unit of cryptguard, leaving only one alive, and then directs the rest of his attacks into the Varghulf, not wanting to wipe the Cryptguard out, and thus allow them to return elsewhere on the board. The Varghulf retaliates and takes the Blightlord down to one health.

credit: Ash Moore

It’s a pretty visual album, not only the sleeve art, which is incredible by the way, but also how the use of samples and evocative dystopian imagery conjures up this AI-ruled hellscape of a future.

We're very imagery orientated. We got in touch with a guy called Mark Cooper and he was amazing. He came up with this incredible painting for the artwork. I think creating a pink Death Metal album sleeve is a real first. Maybe not a first, but it's definitely interesting. 

I mean, we're all nerds really. The whole band is like proper nerds. Everybody's absolutely obsessed with Lord of the Rings. Everybody's obsessed with gaming, Warhammer, Magic The Gathering, There are actual film samples in that album. There's one from Soylent Green, and there's also another from… I can’t remember now. If you listen, audience, and spot it stick it in the comments. 

And as well as all that, there are a lot of Warhammer references in the album too. You've got a song called Genestealer, and a few other references too. What kind of impact does Warhammer have on the story you’re trying to tell, and on all those themes in the album?

I'm the one who’s obsessed with Warhammer.

I wanted to tie together the lexicon of Nurgle and utilize that as a way of doing storytelling within Death Metal. Death Metal has a solid history with Warhammer. If you go all the way back to 1986 you had Bolt Thrower, who are also from the midlands, they named their band after a war machine from Fantasy Battles, as well as bolters in 40k. Realm of Chaos is one of Bolt Thrower’s seminal albums. That mostly mentions World Eaters actually….

There’s a huge history with Warhammer and death metal. There was even a whole Warhammer record label once. They were doing flexi discs and there were a bunch of different bands putting out Warhammer releases. So, one of my goals when starting this band was to continue that. 

But it’s not really strictly about Warhammer, it was more that I was just applying the imagery and the lexicon as a way of being able to express what I wanted to tell through storytelling. We have a song called Metaphysical Maladies. That was a spell by a Plaguecaster in Warhammer. It was a kind of spiritual disease. So, I applied that phrase to some substance abuse problems I've had in the past. I'm over now. But I was able to use that spell name to bring out what I wanted to say.

And then when we got to the Diseased Machine, I was playing a lot of Genestealer Cults in 40k, so obviously the song Genestealer gets its name from that, but that song's actually about nepotism. 

There's also lyrical elements in the Grotesque Union that talk about apotheosis. If you think about demon princes and you think about chaos essentially when they transcend human form into something that's more. I was utilizing that imagery as a vehicle to talk about real world stuff as well. About how people make changes to themselves, like taking drugs that make you lose weight, or people injecting their lips with filler. All of these transhuman elements, beautification elements as well, and the way people worship all.  The way people worship Love Islands on TV. I just find it immoral and I wanted to just say something about that. 

In terms of Warhammer, the way Genestealer Cults infiltrate the hive cities and politics and start to climb the hierarchies is interesting. Then the Day of Ascension comes, and they're absolutely slaughtered by the Tyranids and turned into biofuel. The way in which AI has happened has been the same. It’s cultish. People have been worshipping machines way too much. We're losing our humanity. Mutagenic Host, believe it or not, it's actually a humanistic band, which is quite rare in death metal.

Kieffer Passey

Now it’s my turn to clap back. I manage to finish off the Blightlord with a spell from the Archhregent and then free my Varghulf to go off and see to the Plaguebearers who had snuck on and stole one of my objectives. Then my Morbhegs charge into the big punch up in the middle to kill off as many Blightkings as possible, and then keep the rest of his forces pinned in the middle. I manage to score myself enough points to keep my slim lead.

People often laugh at me when I say Warhammer lore actually has a lot to tell us about the world. But anyone who reads the books knows it's more than just rolling dice and moving plastic around a table.

I'm a Nurgle fanatic. I know you are too. Really, I just cannot shake it away, you know. I can't be rid of it. I play it all; Spearhead, AOS, 40K and Kill Team, and I play Nurgle across everything.

There's just something that’s so real world about Nurgle at the moment. We talk about geotropic diseases, particularly with COVID you know, and then you talk about a lot of ecological problems in the world. It feels like the age of Nurgle.

Yeah, the thing I love the most about Nurgle is that whilst he’s the god of disease and despair, he also gives his followers this kind of fake happiness so that they can endure it. His followers are all really jolly and they've all got big smiles on their faces even as they're rotting to pieces. That's almost what you see happening today. People are getting used to being treated like shit, having their rights and humanity eroded, but they’re being given this false happiness in the form of Love Island or being able to generate pictures of Putin in a bikini with AI or whatever. So, I can see where you're coming from.

Yeah, I mean his followers also refer to him as the Grandfather. So it’s all pretty patriarchal too. He's devoted to his followers, you know, and they'll do anything for him.

And I just feel like today people's freedoms are just being completely eroded and people are subscribing to ways of living that they shouldn't be. Almost as a spell on society. Degradation and rot to make its way in, and I think the mechanizations of society are so rotted now. 

I'm so sick of it. I guess Mutagenic Host has been a way to reflect on those in. In a positive way.

Credit: Kieffer Passey

Ash gets priority once again going into the final round. There isn’t a huge amount he can do now, other than cough on the Morbhegs, killing all but one of them. As predicted at the start, his movement – or lack of – is his downfall.  With only 4” on his Blightkings, retreating wouldn’t let him get enough distance away to claim any more points for the primary.  But when it comes to my final turn, a retreat with my one remaining Morbheg lets me clip the objective deep in his territory, as well as letting me get a guy within three inches of the long battlefield edge, scoring me enough points to finally win the game.

So, how was getting beaten by me?

Oh, mate, I mean, to be fair, getting beat by another Nurgilite is fine, even if you're using Flesh Eater Courts. But that was really well balanced, wasn't it? I think I made a bad move to start with by going first and putting something out on its own. The Morbehg Knights movement is so good that it all came down to movement in the end, like I said it would.  

But that's the only time I've ever lost both Pusgoyles and everything else that lived, they’re pretty tanky, but I should have protected them more. 

The interesting thing about Spearhead is that sometimes it’s very bloody very quick, because those are the cards you've drawn. But I think our battle tactics earlier on favoured a more cagey approach. I think it was round two before we even started fighting.

I think Spearhead is one of the best skirmish games GW has ever made. On the whole it’s really balanced. Some armies are maybe a little too strong, like Slaves to Darkness. Some are really, really weak, like the second Nurgle one. But mostly it’s a lot of fun. Not like Combat Patrol. That’s garbage. 

Also we were able to bring it to a pub and play it!

Why do you think Warhammer and metal go together so well? You don't exactly hear of many Warhammer K Pop bands.

Well, it's the grim, dark element, isn't it? It's the perpetual war. People seem to think that Death Metal fans are obsessed with killing and violence. But actually, really what they are doing is just reflecting real world horrors. They’re mostly lovely people.

And I think that death metal and Warhammer are so intrinsic because although all the visual elements are really married up, you know, demons, gunfire, death, at the same time, at the core of it, I think it's about people trying to deal with traumatic and horrible events. Music and war gaming both have a cathartic nature. Because even though we’re touching on some dark points, we can have fun while doing it.

I've seen you play live, and it's a lot of fun.  It's not miserable, everything's quite tongue in cheek.

Sure. I mean, you know, like the depiction of the end of the world via the onslaught of AI. It's not so much a joke, but it's almost like a pastiche, like a pictorial nonsense thing. I think that's just a natural response to something so horrific.

You have to be like that. Otherwise what are you going to do?

So what’s next for the band?

So we did our first headline tour at the start of the year and that went really well. We did six dates across the UK and that went really well. We'd only really supported bands until that point. And it's kind of a little bit of a big balls move to do a headline tour when you're still not on a major label. But it went really well. 

In July we played Dortmund Deathfest playing with Deicide and Asphyx. Also with Benediction who are another Birmingham based old school death metal band.  We also played alongside 200 Stab Wounds and Sanguisugabogg, which are two great bands, Jungle Rot played too. It’s like playing with Death Metal royalty. But someone over there loved us so got us over. 

But now we’re mostly working on our new album. It’s going to be our magnus opus as a band. It's going to be our most creative. Even in terms of visuals. I think there's going to be things coming out that we're going to try that maybe people haven't done for a long time. This band doesn't really know its limits.

So it's not gonna be the awkward second album. 

Absolutely not. No way. Like, this band only has ever kept the best of what we are that we can achieve. We will never, ever accept mediocrity

Credit: Ash Moore And what are you working on in terms of Warhammer at the moment?

I've been playing a lot of Spearhead. I own maybe 11k worth of Maggotkin of Nurgle and and Death Guard. And I've been painting that now for five years. I'm part of the First Founding club in Chessington, but probably spend more time at Kingston Warhammer Club because I've been there from the start. 

I’ve painted a good 7K of each, but then the new Maggotkin range came out and I kind of just got a little bit tired of painting green and grime, you know, So I actually started doing a couple of Spearheads. I painted Helsmiths of Hashut. I did them in this really bold, clean, copper scheme with red pigment on the base, which makes a difference from the really messy disgusting work with Nurgle. I've also got Iron Jaws Spearhead, so I’m playing a lot of that at the moment.

I mean, having ADHD and being a hobbyist is a challenge. I've just started taking medication at 36. It's really difficult to do Warhammer, so I have to really focus. But with Spearhead I can get one box, paint it up, and be able to play right away, rather than having these huge projects where you have some painted, some not painted, some half painted. You know, it's quite difficult really. For anybody that has neurodivergency, Spearhead's a really great way of doing Warhammer.

Spearhead's also a great way of getting people involved in the hobby. There are lots of kids at my club and we teach them how to play. There's a painting competition where everybody paints Spearhead. Hopefully that burgeons more AOS players as well. 

But it’s a good time for Warhammer in general. I think the 11th edition 40K is going to be really good, and I’m enjoying the new Generals Handbook for AOS too.

title: Devils may cry in this board game about battling personal demons
content:
Board games aren't usually associated with delving into deep "character study" as a tabletop RPG can. That's not to say board games can't hit those personal notes, but the lack of roleplay may seem like an obstacle. However, roleplay is but one way to explore one's mind. Through thoughtful mechanics and theming, board games have proved time and again their introspective potential.

This upcoming board game seals that. Demonically.

Personal Demons by Judson Cowan is a puzzle board game where you must overcome your inner demons through therapeutic ritual. In a wholesome twist on the occult, players work together to overcome those toxic thoughts dwelling within their mind palace. Personally, I like to imagine DnD classes such as Warlock perform similar rituals to keep their patrons in check.

The game makes use of classic occult accoutrement such as seals, cards and sins for its spatial puzzle mechanics. The gameplay loop revolves around revealing personal demons, accruing sins, and using special abilities  to score points against their demons. Every demon has unique abilities, but so does each player depending on their Courage cards. At the end of the game, the player with the most points is celebrated for their progress in battling their demons.

However, the very narrative and mechanics of the game means everyone wins.  Even a bad run does not result in death or some other doomed fate. You end the ritual having learned new ways to fight those inner demons next time. Whether solo or as an addition to your couples board games gallery, this is a fantastic game for meditation. The creator makes no secret of how allegorical of therapy the board game is, and that sentiment is why I was so fascinated in the first place.

Therapy is tough. Even as someone who has undergone it in the past and am deeply thankful for it, there was this nagging feeling I "wasn't doing it right." I changed my perspective, and engaged with therapy not as the ultimate fix, but as "tuning up" my mind. Healing takes time, and approaching each session as progress helped greatly with my outlook. That's what this board game manages to get across through its beautiful and clever design.

You can support Personal Demons on Kickstarter.

If you want some more ritual buddies, the Wargamer Discord has several eager occult enthusiasts.

title: The horse-racing TTRPG inspired by Umamusume is absolutely umazing
content:
Tabletop RPGs, frankly speaking, feel like such an under-represented artform in the fanart space. So many series out there could work so well in a tabletop roleplay setting, whether that's through unique mechanics or just a fascinating world. Despite that, some TTRPGs still floor me with how well they translate to the tabletop.

Especially when said TTRPG is about anime horse girls.

UMA RPG by Laelaps Games is a horsegirl racing TTRPG, a combination of words that should honestly appear more in the history of the English language. Shockingly, it's not even the first attempt at a TTRPG inspired by the anime, but it's certainly one of the most ambitious. Tabletop fans will be quite surprised to see how well the average horsegirl stacks up to the fantastical DnD races.

The strength and speed of these young women easily match that of horses in the real world. As a bonus, they even possess a fey-like beauty, all the way to enrapturing audiences with concerts after a victorious race. Speaking of, their culture revolves almost exclusively to racing, each young horsegirl fated to run forever forward. That should give you an idea of how seriously these equine ladies take the sport. The game faithfully brings the intensity of training and racing horsegirls to the tabletop.

It also explains why The UMA RPG does not take half-measures in its interpretation. Though you only need the humble d6, there's a surprising amount of mechanical depth from training to racing. Even so, it was designed for even TTRPG newbies to get into. Instead of the complexity of  DnD classes, character creation revolves around a universal pool of stats, hobbies, and talents.

But for my horse-betting money,  the most fun mechanics come straight from the meat of the game: racing. The impressively designed race tracks and multiple race phases capture the moment-to-moment tension perfectly. If you're at all a fan of Umamusume, you owe it to yourself to check this game out. And even if you aren't, there's a genuinely compelling sports-themed TTRPG here for you to enjoy.

You can check out the UMA RPG for free on itch.io.

If the UMA RPG's got you in a great mood for more tabletop hijinks, the Wargamer Discord has plenty to share.
