title: BattleTech IlClan List Overview: Jade Falcon Remnant
content:
Howdy everyone and welcome to List Overview. BattleTech has a great many factions in it, with 31 factions with IlClan availability lists on Master Unit List. These factions all have their quirks, idiosyncrasies, oddball unique units, and long-running fandom stereotypes about their playstyles. As a new player it can be somewhat hard to figure out what a Jade Falcon list is supposed to be like, what a Clan Protectorate list looks like, what much of anything looks like. In addition, many players have somewhat of an odd opinion that a list is either competitively viable or its fluffy, faction appropriate, and lore friendly. The idea that a list can be both very strong and extremely on theme for a faction seems to escape a lot of people. Today we are going to demonstrate this by looking at an on-theme, powerful list for the Jade Falcon Remnant, one of the most interesting factions come IlClan (in my humble opinion).

Lore Primer

The Jade Falcon Epsilon Galaxy forces from Battletech Aces: Scouring Sands. Credit: Jack Hunter

The Jade Falcon Remnant, also sometimes called the Sudeten Falcons or Jiyi’s Falcons, are a splinter group of Clan Jade Falcon, rejecting their clan’s defeat by Clan Wolf and acting with rather un-clanlike wisdom and tact to secure their position and their ownership of the planet Sudeten. The Jade Falcon Remnant are in the unique position of having more mechs than pilots, desperately trying to fill their ranks. This includes straight up stealing a class of cadets from the Ghost Bears in quite possibly one of the funniest raids in all of BattleTech fiction. Khan Jiyi Chistu is a really fantastic character in one of BattleTech’s most interesting subsettings (The Hinterlands), and the Jade Falcon Remnant (or at least part of a Jade Falcon Remnant its unclear) star as the opposing force in the BattleTech Aces: Scouring Sands box. 

You might be interested in playing the Jade Falcon Remnant if you want to have some of the best color schemes in the game, if you hate Clan Wolf almost as much as I do, and/or if you really like Thunderbolts, Thors, and Turkinas.

Availability

The Jade Falcon Remnants have one of the best Mech availabilities in the IlClan era, with access to best-in-class OmniMechs like the Butcherbird(Ion Sparrow), Phantom, Stormcrow, Turkina, Mad Dog(Vulture) MkIV, Loki MkII, and Blood Asp. In addition, the Jade Falcon Remnants have access to several high quality and exclusive (or near exclusive) standard BattleMechs, such as the Thunderbolt C 2, Shrike 2, Thunderbolt IIC, and the Jade Hawk. You will struggle to build a wall of steel or any other strategy that hinges on large amounts of cheap armor, but the Jade Falcon Remnant is extremely good at playing either high speed cavalry beatdown strategies with their strong stable of 5/8 heavy mechs, or, as we will demonstrate today, at simply doing so much damage so quickly that many lists simply cannot withstand them for long enough for it to matter.

The List

Our thematic Scale 4 (8000 BV) list today consists of the following mechs:

  • Turkina H, 4/5, 2712 BV
  • Thunderbolt C 2, 4/5, 2170 BV
  • Phantom H, 4/5, 1178 BV
  • Locust IIC 4, 3/5, 954 BV
  • Butcherbird (Ion Sparrow) C, 4/4, 978 BV

Coming in at a grand total of 7992 BV, this list combines high speed “Buzzsaw” strikers with a solid, high damage heavy mech and one of the game’s premium centerpiece assault mechs.

Turkina H

Clan Jade Falcon Turkina B. Credit: Valk

The Turkina H is a high quality assault mech, weighing 95 tons and moving 3/5/3 with a frightening weapon load consisting of paired UAC/10s, paired MPLs, and a trio of heavy medium lasers. All of these weapons are helped by the Targeting Computer mounted, bizarrely, in the right arm. The Turkina H has effectively no heat issues, only going up 1+movement on a run. 

You need to deploy your centerpiece carefully here, as 3/5/3 is just not a particularly impressive movement profile. The jump jets can help with getting in to a firing position, but with so much damage tied up in heavy medium lasers you want to be pushing forwards to get in the fight as quickly as possible. Find an open line that gets you to the middle of the battlefield in a timely fashion and slam the Turkina down it. Our wobbly idiot bird son will take his time getting there and is no good at all for objectives, but if you can leverage the thick armor and great close ranged firepower you should be able to find some good success with him.

Thunderbolt C 2

Thunderbolt. Credit: porble

A mech that is, in IlClan, exclusive to the Jade Falcon Remnant, the Thunderbolt C 2 has rapidly become one of my favorites. It carries a good armor load, a standard engine, moves 4/6/0, and has a pretty fantastic weapon set. An ERPPC is the only concession to true long range, with the rest of the mech being set up for close range brawling with 4 ER Medium Lasers, a streak SRM 6, 2 ER Small Lasers for a good reason, a pair of Small Pulse Lasers, and an AMS. While in the past we have ragged on AMS somewhat, in the new core rules AMS is quite good, massively reducing the damage output of missile weapons. As ATMs and Clan LRMs are some of the game’s premium ways to puke damage, this damage reduction is very noticeable against things that would otherwise be natural predators of the Thunderbolt C 2. 

With a good firing pattern of “Everything but the PPC”, the Thunderbolt C 2 really wants to get to close combat and stick there. Put it on the same ingress line as the Turkina H, but try to not outpace Mr Turkey too much. A standard engine is nice, but 65 tons is not heavy enough to take aggro from an entire enemy list for very long. Neither of these mechs are particularly subtle, but they are easy to use. Front Towards Enemy. Which is something I should really paint on the mini-fridge that is the chest of a Thunderbolt.

Locust IIC 4 and Phantom H

Jade Falcon Epsilon Galaxy Locust IIC 4. Credit: Jack Hunter

Putting these mechs together because they have very nearly the same weapon load. The Phantom is much, much more durable as well as faster, but the Locust IIC is cheaper. Both carry 6 heavy small lasers as their primary weapons, with the Phantom backing that up with an MPL and a flamer. The Locust IIC 4 instead has an ER medium laser, which is a bit of a bummer but shouldn’t make much of a difference in practice. These mechs are very simple in use cases, they want to get next to something and puke 43 points of laser damage into it. That said, within that simple use case there are a few things to keep in mind.

The key one is to keep it in your pants. These mechs do a LOT of damage and they are very, very fast, but this can lead you towards poor play. You do not want these mechs to engage early, you only want these mechs to get involved in the fight once your Turkina and Thunderbolt are already taking fire. After that you want to make absolutely sure that the slow movers remain at all times the more tempting targets, ensuring 4 TMM (or 3 TMM plus Terrain) on your strike package. If they are the best or only shot an enemy has, they will die immediately. Most players are not going to be able to ignore a Turkina they are hitting on 7s to risk firing at a Phantom on 10s, but if the shots approach being equal you will rapidly find yourself down half your mechs. 

In addition, the Phantom is your only fast mover with hands, so depending on the scenario you might end up sending it off to do objectives. If this is the case you need to be even more careful with your Locust, as you can rapidly end up without a significant ground-bound backstabbing force.

Butcherbird (Ion Sparrow) C

Clan Jade Falcon Ion Sparrow Prime. Credit: Valk.

I am going to call this the Butcherbird from here, because that name is cooler. The Butcherbird C is one of the game’s best light mechs (and was voted such in our article on the topic by multiple people). Carrying 6 ER small lasers slaved to a Tcomp with a 8/12/10 movement profile, the Butcherbird C does whatever the hell it wants. Ideally it wants to mirror the Locust IIC and the Phantom, going for backstabs and picking off targets who are tied up tangling with the heavy hitters. Beyond that it has much more agency than either of the other strikers, being capable of rapidly responding to literally anything and being more than capable as a light mech hunter, freely bullying offending Spiders and Fire Moths.

Assuming the scenario doesn’t care about having hands, this is also your premium objective dork. 10 hexes of jump is just incredible mobility. Even without any EWAR equipment, probes, ECM, the like, that speed on its own will cover a good chunk of the core book scenarios, particularly against a slower opponent. If the scenario doesn’t require attention, 30 damage at -1 to hit is 30 damage at -1 to hit, go mess some people up.

Gameplan

At this point you should be seeing what this list’s overall gameplan and win condition is. The light mechs hang back while the big boys push up to the center of the map to take control of the center, and after a fight has begun in mid around them the strikers descend and snap at the heels and flanks of any of the enemy’s mechs that seem vulnerable. If anything tries to back down or get away from the frontline, dive it with the fast movers and see how they like over 100 points of laser damage coming in while they are vulnerable.

This list is capable of horrifying damage output and can play many objectives fairly well due to the 3 high speed assets. Your goal should be to apply that horrifying damage to melt down the enemy’s heavies and assaults, trading positively into them by virtue of not giving them enough time to extract their BV out of your list. You are capable of doing more than 220 points of damage in a single turn, more damage than the majority of heavy mechs have armor. If they try to outrange you and refuse to go to the middle of the board try to dive any snipers or long range specialists with your light mechs. While doing this, push onto their side of the map and pin them up against the board edge while Turkina-ing all over the place.

It isn’t an undefeatable list though. If your enemy invests in a few premium light mech hunters (Gunsmith, Cicada 4A, etc) you can quickly lose your mobility advantage if you aren’t careful. A traditional wall of steel might also give you some issues, assuming your opponent invested in precision autocannons and pulse lasers. A Precision AC/20 to any part of your light strikers will likely kill or cripple them, and LPLs are similarly threatening. After the light mechs are gone, you are only a few unlucky rolls away from being out of the game and a well made wall of steel will make a lot of rolls. It isn’t a hard counter, but it can be very hard to approach with your fast movers.

That said, this all assuming a general melee with no real objectives. So, how does this list play the Core Book Missions?

Core Missions

Jade Falcon force from the Battletech Core Box. Credit: Jack Hunter

The core missions are divided into two categories. They are either broadly just deathmatches with funky deployment, or they are ones that have objective points to control in various ways. The kill missions will be pretty easy for this list and you can mostly play them as above, but the objective missions all require a bit more thought.

For Deathmatches, the core book has:

  • Ambush - If you roll attacker, divide the slow from the fast and put the slow on the side with the quicker route to center
  • Annihilation - Literally just a deathmatch do whatever
  • Dominate - Kill mission, but you can leave the board from the enemy's side to score as if you had killed your own mech that just moved off the table. Do this if a mech is damaged to the point you aren't getting any value out of it.
  • Extraction - If you roll defender, put your big boys in the middle and move the fast movers on. Play as normal
  • Focal Point - Technically an objective mission but this is a straight forwards king of the hill mission. Move your big mechs on the fastest line to the point, try to score it turn 1 with your fast movers if you can before backing them down.
  • General Melee - Slightly funny kill mission. Put your big mechs in the center and play as normal.

As for Objective missions, things are a bit more diverse. The book has the following objective centric missions:

  • Control the Field - Straight forwards objective sitting mission. Goal should be to sit the Turkina on whichever backfield objective has a stronger position for it, as the UAC/10s and MPLs give it acceptable range. The thunderbolt will want to push to the objective opposite it, supported by your fast movers. Once you are racking up points from that, send your striker package to try to claim the other enemy objective while the Turkina (hopefully) keeps the enemy off of its objective. You need to sacrifice your other home objective, you do not have the numbers to hold both.
  • Hold The Line - Straight forwards objective mission. Put the Turkina on the objective closest to your board edge (or the more defensible one if multiple are equidistant) and shove everything else forwards onto whichever other objective seems easier to take. Make sure your Turkina is in a position to support them with its big guns.
  • Objective Raid - I hate this mission. Pray that you don't get scammed by potential objectives while your little mechs skitter around scanning. Move your big mechs up to whatever objectives are closest, and if you roll Mobile objectives try to use the Thunderbolt and Phantom to pull objectives into a ball next to your Turkina.
  • Sensor Check - Run next to the enemy with your light mechs and scan them. Once you have scanned enough that you feel you have done enough, pull your light mechs off the table. Try to distract anything with pulse or precision with your big mechs to avoid total light mech elimination.
  • Steel Rain - Roll attacker. If you don't roll attacker, drop the big mechs first and the light mechs second. Get your bigs onto a pair of objectives that are near each other, and have the Phantom and Thunderbolt consolidate objectives as in Objective Raid. If you roll attacker, try to get the Phantom off the board with an objective ASAP. This will get your racking up points for minimum cost while you try to focus down whatever enemy unit/concentration seems the most vulnerable.
  • Urban Sweep - Run your light mechs around and scan all the objectives. Push your big boys up an obvious line and kill anything fast enough to scan well. Killing probe mechs is also a good idea. This mission is somewhat non-interactive, you both just spin to win and see who actually wins VP from the objectives.

Final Thoughts

This list is trying to use some Falcon specific/iconic units while still having a coherent focus. Thors, Thor IIs, Lokis, and Loki MkIIs are well and good, but it can be difficult to build an effective list around them given their low damage for BV. The Turkina is an excellent centerpiece and it commands attention at the table while being the biggest dumbest bird to ever live. The Thunderbolt C 2 is a mech that I desperately need to be on more availabilities, it is not fair that a heavy mech this good is stuck on Jade Falcon.

Clan forces at Scale 4 (8000 BV) struggle sometimes to fill a full star...if you want to only use big mechs. The Clan Light and Medium mech stable is in general very strong in IlClan across all Clans, and the Falcon Remnant have a particularly good selection. The Phantom on its own very nearly makes a top tier fast mover stable on its own, with the Butcherbird, Hammerhead, and Stormcrow just adding on to it. You need to really consider taking lighter and somewhat thinner assets at 8000 compared to, say, 10000, but you can still squeeze in any big boy fairly easily. When your cheap mechs are some of the best in the game, its not a problem to splurge on the best of the really expensive ones.

Overall I really am happy with this list and I think you could put in some very good results with it. This is just a starting point and my word is not law (yet) and I make no claim that this is the only way to play Falcons, but it is one of the better ways to play Clans in general at 8K as a result of the above mentioned very high quality of fast, cheap Clan mechs come IlClan. I’d love to hear any thoughts, opinions, expansions, or alterations to this list.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: How to Paint Everything: Ultramarines Space Marines (Updated September 25, 2026)
content:
This article is part of a larger series on how to paint Space Marines. To return to that series, click here.

In our How to Paint Everything series, we take a look at how to paint well, everything, with a look at different methods from different artists. In this article we're looking at what is perhaps the most famous of space marine chapters and the face of Warhammer 40,000: The Ultramarines.

Changelog

  • Update (Latest): 2026-09-23 Updated to include reference photos including the names of colors used.
  • Update: 2023-11-23 Format streamlined.
  • Published: 2022-01-05

Covered in this Article

  • Schemes from different painters for how to paint the Salamanders, including the chapter's Pre-Heresy look.
  • Tips on how to paint the Ultramarines Primarch, Roboute Guilliman
  • Notes on the heraldry and iconography of the Ultramarines

Ultramarines Heraldry - Click to Expand

Ultramarines are the Codex Chapter, and as such they follow all the heraldic conventions laid down by Roboute himself. This makes for a lot of fun opportunities for little details and visual interest, such as distinguishing a squad of veterans with white helmets, or picking out a specific sergeant as a veteran with a red helmet and white stripe, or individual squad markings, etc. The adherence to codex markings is actually one of my favorite things about the Chapter because it adds some visual variety and also helps you tell micro-stories as you paint your squads and models. Ultramarines are vaguely Greco-Roman, and as such you can also make good use of certain motifs like laurels or helmet crests to help set models or units apart.

Credit: SRM

Our Guide to Painting Space Marine Heraldry the Codex Astartes has everything you need to know about painting Codex-compliant chapters, with a particular focus on the Ultramarines.

Another option when thinking about heraldry is to use an alternative color scheme for a unit or set of units to distinguish them on the battlefield. Fellow Goonhammer author SRM has made great use of this for his Vanguard Marines by painting them in a scheme reminiscent of the Ultramarines Destroyer Scheme from the Horus Heresy. This gives the models a very distinct look while also looking cohesive with the rest of his force; you can learn more about it here.

Painting Ultramarines

Alfredo's Method - Click to Expand

This was written when I had recently painted Veteran Battle Brothers Argentus and Auralius to accompany leaders of the chapter into battle. These models offer a lot of great details and opportunities for different techniques.

Step 0: Planning and Assembly

For any project, you want to have a plan! This was particularly the case for these two models because their cloaks were broken up in such a way that I couldn't feasibly paint them in subassemblies without (even uglier) seams when I was done (aside from heads and backpacks). With that in mind, I decided I would spray three main colors, blue for the armor, red for the cloaks, and metal for the swords, in that order and mask in between to protect previous steps.

Another important consideration was the inside of the cloaks. I chose not to glue the models to their bases while working on them so that I could pull them off and get at the space between their legs. This is good to keep in mind for any model with a cape or cloak. I did not think of this when I built my first squad of Skitarii, and it was... not fun.

Because the models consist of two main colors, blue and red, I took some time to think about how I wanted to paint those. I have a standard recipe for Ultramarine armor I use (scroll down), and I, of course, wanted to stick with that so they'd fit in with the rest of the army, so I needed the red to work with that. I find the red that 'Eavy Metal uses for Ultra's cloaks to be a bit too bold and vibrant for my tastes, particularly since my army is quite battle-worn.

I decided to go with a deep purple base for the red in order to tie it back to the purple tones of the blue and create some cohesion between these otherwise very different colors, and then bring the red up all the way to a bright ochre, without tinting it too far towards orange with highlights. The goal was to create some nice contrast between the red and blue while unifying them with purple shadows and also ensuring that the blue was the most saturated color on the model; they're Ultramarines, after all.

If I could go back and do one thing differently, I'd be a bit more conservative in how I welded the seams on the cloaks. I use a mix of Tamiya Clear and melted sprue to create a liquid filler, but I went a bit overboard in my application, and you can see actual seam welds in several areas, which isn't ideal. So while the idea is sound, you really want to make sure you're not applying too much and take the time to sand and smooth down the seams to get a nice finish.

Step 1: Priming

I went with a black-to-white zenithal highlight for the pair. I wanted to maximise the contrast between the armor shadowed by the cape and the bright blue of their exposed pauldrons and helmets.

Step 2: Basecoating

Credit: Alfredo Ramirez

For the blue armor, I went way off the reservation and used a Reaper Master Series Triad called... Ultramarine Blues. Crazy, right? As you can (hopefully) see, the darkest color in the triad has some nice purple tones, and overall the triad is quite vibrant and blue.

Credit: Alfredo Ramirez

Unlike most Space Marine models, the Victrix Guard have two very large areas of color, the armor and their capes. Rather than basecoat the capes by hand, I wanted to paint some nice and smooth gradients with the airbrush, so I masked off all the armor with a combination of Tamiya Tape and Masking Putty.

In order to create strong contrast between the light and dark areas of the cape while also unifying the shadows with the armor, I sprayed the entire cape with Vallejo Game Air Hexed Lichen, which is a dark and deep purple, and then sprayed Vallejo Game Air Bloody Red from a high angle. Using a very small needle, I was then able to get some very thin highlights on some of the folds of the cape with Vallejo Model Color Yellow Ochre. My cape was now going from purple to yellow, so in order to unify the whole thing, I sprayed it with some thinned Scale75 Inktense Red.

There were relatively few colors left to basecoat:

  • Gold: My usual recipe for Ultras is Scalecolor Decayed Metal as a base, followed by covering most areas with Scalecolor Necro Gold and then highlighted with Scalecolor Dwarven Gold.
  • White: For some of the white, I stole a trick from fellow Goonhammer author (and resident Dadhammer expert) Lupe and used a mixture of Vallejo Model Color Light Sea Grey, which is a nice cool off-white with fantastic coverage, and white Artist's Ink from Daler Rowney. This gave me a nice smooth white in 2-3 coats. For the big Ultimas on the shields, I ended up re-masking the model and cheating with an airbrush, using a progression of Reaper Snow Shadow, Reaper Ghost White and Vallejo Model Air Insignia White to get some nice and smooth blends on the larger area. Masking might sound like a lot of work, but I promise it's not and can ultimately save a lot of time for tricky colors like white, red or yellow.
  • Other Colors: For the rest of the details, I used my usual Vallejo Model Color Dark Rust for the leather, Vallejo Model Color Cavalry Brown for the aiguillette across the chest, Vallejo Model Color Buff for the parchment and Vallejo Model Color Magenta for the purity seal wax.

Step 3: Washing

Before washes, I applied decals on the gloss-coated model. See JD's section below for details on how best to apply decals.

Washing was pretty simple. A pin wash of a black/burnt umber mixture (giving me a warm black to contrast with the cool blue) on the armor and deepest shadows of the cloak, and all-over washes of burnt umber on the gold and other details. The interior of the cloak got an all-over wash, which I then cleaned up with some white spirits.

Step 4: Highlighting

Highlighting follows my usual process. I start by highlighting every armor edge with Scalecolor Sky Blue, which is a nice vibrant and bright blue. I then hit top-facing edges with Vallejo Model Color Sky Blue, which is a much lighter color despite having the same name. Finally, I hit corners and compound edges with Vallejo Model Color Blue Grey Pale.

Step 5: Weathering

My Ultramarines are typically weathered in three stages:

  • Using a piece of sponge, I apply Scalecolor Trash Metal first and then Vallejo Model Color German Camo Black Brown to areas of wear such as the top of the helmet, shoulder pads, feet, hands, etc.
  • Take some dark umber pigment powder and mix it with pigment medium to create a runny paste. I then apply this to some of the recesses on the legs and feet to show areas where mud has built up and dried.
  • Once that is dry, I apply dry pigments to the legs to get a dusty effect. Depending on what I'm going for, I might do this more than once with applications of matte varnish at very low PSI in between.

Finished!

Credit: Alfredo Ramirez

With these models being so similar, I chose to use a little bit of heraldry to differentiate them in my head and give them some backstory. Brother Argentus was recently promoted to the Victrix Guard after the death of one of his predecessors, and you can identify him by his Vigilus Campaign Badge (peeking out behind the shield on his right greave). Brother Auralius, on the other hand, is a 2nd-generation Primaris who underwent the Calgarian Rites and has served the chapter for well over a century. His left greave is decorated with a much older Campaign Badge, commemorating his valor in a joint action with the Crimson Fists a long way away from Vigilus.

RichyP's Method - Click to Expand

As is becoming standard, RichyP brings us yet another shamefully fast take on our Chapter of choice with great results!

Another quick paint job that looks good from tabletop distance. Note this model has had 2 failed paint jobs underneath it, so some of the details are a little more clogged than I’d have liked, but it works well enough to demonstrate it.

Step 1: Base Coat

After priming the model grey, cover it in thinned Warhammer Macragge Blue (it took 2 quick passes with a size 3 brush to get an even coverage)

Step 2: Rough Highlight 1

For this step, thin some Warhammer Russ Grey and do some thin lines around the prominent edges. They’ll look quite stark against the Macragge Blue, but the even starker inner highlight later will actually make it look less overpowering (as counter-intuitive as that sounds).

Step 3: Adding a bit of Contrast

Take some Warhammer Nuln Oil and mix it with Contrast Medium, mix it about 1:2 (1 part Nuln to 2 parts Contrast Medium). Now cover all the blue areas. I switched to a different background here for some unknown reason.

Step 4: Edge Highlight 2

My favourite bit after the owl painting section is this bit. I used Warhammer Blue Horror for this stage, but Warhammer Ulthuan Grey would probably work equally as well if you’re not an edging enthusiast. Take the colour and thin it with water until it almost breaks, then it’s ready to use. Using a smaller brush (I used a 1 for this bit), draw some smaller lines inside the previous highlights, and it’ll make it look like the blue is glossy.

Step 5: Black-Lining

Thin some Warhammer Abaddon Black (again, get it to the point where it almost separates) and apply it in the deepest recesses, and cover any metallic areas or anything that will actually be black (in this case, the gun). The thinned black will pool in the recesses over the grey primer and give you a cheap shade and base coat in one. Not pictured in this step, I also painted the eyes with the previous mix of Warhammer Blue Horror (I also did the plasma coil the same).

Step 6: The Devil’s in the Details

This step looks like there’s a lot of work involved; there really isn’t, but because of the amount of little bits, I’ve bundled them into one step.

Paint scratches in the thinned black from the previous step, and paint the under-edge of the lines in the same Warhammer Blue Horror colour from the previous step to give yourself a fake 3d scratch.

Paint the eye sockets in orange, and dot the same Blue Horror in the back corners. Write some text, U Symbols squad markings, etc., also using the same Blue Horror colour. (I did a couple of red bits too for variety and to tie in with the eye lenses). Cover the plasma coil in Warhammer Aethermatic Blue Contrast, and deliberately go outside the lines to fake a glow.

Edge the pads in gold or whichever company colour you’re aiming for. (I used Scalecolor Elven Gold and blended it with some silver while it was wet).

Don’t forget to paint GH on the shoulder to show your allegiance.

JD's Method - Click to Expand

Self-deprecating introduction aside, JD paints some fantastic-looking Ultramarines that look like they popped off the 'Eavy Metal box art. With this in-depth breakdown, you too can have an 'Eavy Metal Ultramarine army!*

So you want to know how to paint Ultramarines? What can I say that you don’t already know, or can’t look up yourself? Did you fall in love with Games Workshop’s box art? Do you like following the rules, and have no imagination of your own? Then maybe this is the tutorial for you!

I haven’t been part of this hobby long when compared to some of the other hobbyists on here, but the time I have spent within it has been devoted almost entirely to painting Ultramarines, so hopefully this article will help you avoid some of the mistakes I made. Over time, I have done my best to mimic the ‘Eavy Metal style you see on the box art, and I am here to say anyone can do it given the following: practice, steady hands, and good eyesight. No artistic talent required, trust me!

I started painting my Ultramarines back in 2014 (maybe?), and didn’t even use the now-standard Games Workshop scheme until 2015. As any veteran painter can sympathize I view all models from this era as total trash that belongs in a dumpster. While this is overly critical of my previous work, it is important for a painter to have a constant desire to improve. I feel the steps I will list are perhaps the maximum effort I am willing to expend when it comes to painting line troops and vehicles in my army, which is admittedly already very time-intensive. There are further techniques such as airbrush highlighting and blending that can take everything here one step further, so don’t hesitate to introduce them if you have that extra time to burn.

Step 1: PREPARATION!

Before you even begin to paint your models, here are some steps that everyone should take regardless of whether they are painting Ultramarines.

A. Subassemblies: These are important for a couple of reasons. 1) If you fully assemble a model, you’re often going to find that you aren’t going to get 100% coverage with your basecoat if you’re using a rattle can (in this case, Macragge Blue Spray). Not fully assembling the model will allow the paint to hit those areas you might otherwise have trouble hitting and keep that undercoat consistent model-wide. 2) Keeping your model broken up will also allow you to get to details with your brush that might be harder to reach on a fully painted model. How many times have you tried to paint the aquila on the chest of a marine, only to get gold on his boltgun, which he is clutching tightly to his bosom?

B. Taping: This is done concurrently with sub-assembling and is just as important. Use an X-Acto Knife to cut out small pieces of painter’s tape to cover the connection areas of the sub-assemblies. This is important because paint over these areas will make it hard for the glue to hold the final model together, and because GW’s current line of models fit together so perfectly, the undercoat can prevent the model from coming together as intended.

C. Pinning (keeping your dirty nerd hands from ruining your work): For this you want some paperclips and wine corks. What you then do is drill a VERY SHALLOW hole into a non-visible part of the model like the bottom of a foot, gun barrel, or connection point and then use a small amount of super glue to attach a clipped piece of paper clip to it. You then suspend the assembly upwards by push the other end of the paper clip into the cork.

Step 2: Painting time!

So here is the ‘Eavy Metal recipe, but this leaves out some important information on how each of these steps is accomplished, which I will attempt to expand on.

Author’s Note: I do not 100% copy the colors outlined by ‘Eavy Metal, but as you can see from my pictures, they are basically a match. Feel free to use either color scheme, and just focus on my tips for applying progressively lighter edge highlights. You’ll notice that in the above picture, steps 4-6 are merely described as “edge highlight”, which doesn’t convey the differences in each step.

A. Basecoat Macragge Blue – The best way to accomplish this is using the GW rattle can. It is going to provide very even coverage, and doesn’t even require a primer. If you want, you can go over the bottle with Chaos Black primer and then follow it up with the Blue spray. This can be useful if you wish to ensure no grey areas are exposed; however, it isn’t necessary as long as you are being thorough in how you apply the Macragge Blue.

Author’s Note: I tend to finish my bases before I begin the model itself, and use a GW painting handle to prevent paint from being rubbed off.

B. Recess shade with Nuln Oil – I use a GW glaze brush to shade every recess of the model. This can be time-consuming, but I find it more efficient than an all-over wash, since you don’t have to go back and brighten all the armor panels.

C. Thick Edge Highlight of Calgar Blue – What does this mean? Basically, you’re looking for a line of paint less than 1mm wide on all armor panel edges. Perhaps the most important aspect of edge highlighting is maintaining consistent width throughout the model. You may have to go back and use Macragge Blue to tidy up, but be patient because this is perhaps the LONGEST and most important step to this technique.

D. Thin Edge Highlight of Fenrisian Grey – Much of a repeat of the previous step, but you are covering slightly less of the area than in the previous step, and your lines are noticeably thinner, less than half the width of the Calgar Blue, and covering about 50-75% of the edge area, focusing on the raised portions.

E. Corner Highlight of 50:50 Fenrisian Grey and White Scar – This is a final highlight meant to make the sharpest edges stand out and should focus on corners and only the apex of rounded areas such as the knee pads. These might seem too bright, but will become slightly dulled down by the final varnish spray used to protect the finished model.

I have only outlined the steps for painting the blue armor in detail; however, the techniques used for these portions also apply to the metal, gold, and black areas of the model.

  • Black Portions – Base: Abaddon Black > Edge: Mechanicus Standard Grey > Thin Edge: Administratum Grey
  • Metal Portions – Base: Leadbelcher > All-over Shade: Nuln Oil > Edge: Stormhost Silver
  • Gold Portions – Base: Retributor Armour > All-over Shade: Reikland Fleshshade > Edge: Auric Armour Gold > Thin Edge: Stormhost Silver

Step 3: Final Touches

If you have completed the above 4 main portions of the model, congratulations, you’re in the home stretch. When it comes to the purity seals and bolter optics, I merely used the tutorials available on Games Workshop’s Youtube page. For the eye lenses, I applied Ceramite White, making sure to keep it out of the recesses, and then used a glaze of which color I wanted them to appear. This method creates excellent results and can be much less frustrating than trying the same method that is used on weapon optics.

For the insignia if you haven’t been blessed with the secrets to applying transfers I will outline it for you here.

  • Buy Micro Sol and Micro Set
  • Apply Micro Set to the surface you want to apply the transfer to.
  • Apply the transfer to the area using water.
  • Apply Micro Sol to the transfer in small amounts, letting it dry each time. Each application should see the transfer become noticeably softer and softer until it adheres smoothly to the surface
  • Let the transfer dry fully.

Now for the finishing touch. At this point you’ve likely invested a lot of time into the model, and ensuring it remains protected is the final step. I use both a gloss and matte spray varnish to protect my models, specifically, Model Master’s Gloss and Lusterless sprays. The conditions for varnishing your model should be the same as those you used to undercoat it. Apply a single coat of the gloss varnish first; this will provide a thick coat to help protect your model. It is important to note that this stuff comes out thick, even with a quick pass over, so don’t overdo it. Once it dries, you will notice your model looks like it just went through a car wash and wax treatment. Now apply a coat of the Matte/Lusterless Spray. Once it dries, decide if you want to dull it down with another coat. BE CAREFUL at this stage not to overdo it, as you don’t want to dull your model’s brightness to a state below how they looked when you initially painted them.

Campbell McLaughlin's Method - Click to Expand

I have a feeling my method is going to align fairly closely with JD’s, as we’re likely working from the same half-forgotten White Dwarf from ages ago. I will not be covering basing; we have other articles for that. The most important step in my process, and one you’ll see appear whenever I do edge highlights, is the cleanup stage. Always try for crisp highlights, but if you clean up any shaky lines after the fact with a thinned version of your basepaint, you’ll get cleaner results. This step will also be useful later for cleaning up wherever recess shades may have spilt over.

Step 1. Basecoat

We’re going to start with a basecoat of Macragge Blue spray, although you could prime black and paint over with Macragge Blue from a bottle for the same effect.

Step 2. Blue Armor

This is the most important step, so we’ll get it out of the way first. We’ll start by recess shading any details with Nuln Oil, giving them depth and shadow. After this, we highlight each and every edge with Calgar Blue, then hit the sharpest edges with Fenrisian Grey. I also do this around the inside edge of the shoulder pads. 

  • Blue Armor

    • Basecoat: Macragge Blue
    • Recess Shade: Nuln Oil
    • Edge Highlight: Calgar Blue
    • Extreme Edge Highlight: Fenrisian Grey

Step 3. Gold

Blue without gold is like peanut butter without jelly, and a warm gold will balance the cool blue of the armor nicely. I would advise using two thinned coats of Retributor Armour, as all metallic paints are prone to clumping. We’ll wash the chest aquila and anything with detail, like reliquaries or laurels, with Reikland Fleshshade. I usually don’t wash the armor trim unless there are rivets to wash around or an overlapping lip. We’ll then edge highlight it all with Liberator Gold, and hit the sharpest corners with Stormhost Silver to get a gleaming gold. I sometimes skip the Liberator Gold step, but the Stormhost Silver step has a lot of impact.

  • Gold

    • Basecoat: Retributor Armour
    • Recess Shade: Reikland Fleshshade
    • Edge Highlight: Liberator Gold
    • Extreme Edge Highlight: Stormhost Silver

Step 4. Steel

There’s plenty of metal on any given Marine that will fit in this category - some doodads on the helmet, chains, weapon details, and more besides. You can also change up the skulls in the chest aquilas with steel to make them stand out more. I sometimes find it helpful to paint these black first just to outline them, but consider that step optional. From there it’s just a base, an all-over wash, and a highlight, done. You could also use this for the armor undersuit.

  • Steel

    • Basecoat: Leadbelcher
    • All-Over Shade: Nuln Oil
    • Edge Highlight: Stormhost Silver

Step 5. Black Undersuit, Weapons, and Armor

We’re going to paint the undersuit, weapon stocks, and, in some cases, weapon casings black, highlighting it with grey. We’ll be keeping this grey neutral to fit with the color scheme. Too cool and it would blend in, too warm and it would look out of place. Feel free to use whatever black you like here - I like P3’s, but if you wanted something flatter, you could use Pro Acryl Coal Black, or you could use Abaddon Black.

  • Black Details

    • Basecoat: P3 Thamar Black 
    • Edge Highlight: Eshin Grey
    • Extreme Edge Highlight: Dawnstone
Ultramarines Incursors. Credit: SRM

While this doesn’t appear on these models, black armor is a feature on Chaplains, and I like to paint black elements on my Phobos models. For this, I go for a different, cooler black, using the same final highlight color to better tie it in with the blue armor.

  • Black Armor

    • Basecoat: P3 Thamar Black 
    • Edge Highlight: Dark Reaper
    • Extreme Edge Highlight: Fenrisian Grey

Step 6. Red Armor and Weapon Casings

There are people who paint their weapon casings in bright primary colors, and there are people who are cowards. Choose wisely. Obviously you could go with black here - I vary my weapon casings up a lot for fun’s sake - but I generally like red for maximum impact. Much like my process for blue, this will involve a base color, some targeted recess shades, edge highlights and cleanup. On these Bladeguard, I only used this technique for the Veteran Sergeant’s helmet and heraldry across the squad, but normally use it on my boltguns and other weapons.

  • Red Details

    • Basecoat: Mephiston Red
    • Recess Shade: Nuln Oil
    • Edge Highlight: Wild Rider Red
    • Extreme Edge Highlight: Fire Dragon Bright

Step 7. White Armor

A common mistake is to start with a pure white here, but if you do that, there’s nowhere to highlight up to! Instead, we’ll start with a lighter off-white and highlight up. Ulthuan Grey is a great color that covers well over blue, so we’ll slap that down, thin some Nuln Oil down for a recess shade, then highlight that with Pro Acryl Titanium White. I use this on the 1st company trim and helmets, as well as some heraldry and unit markings.

  • White Armor

    • Basecoat: Ulthuan Grey
    • Recess Shade: 1:1 Nuln Oil and water or Lahmian Medium
    • Edge Highlight: Pro Acryl Titanium White

Step 8. Yellow Armor and Weapon Casings

I use yellow often with my heraldry and weapon casings, so if you want to follow my lead, I’ll tell you how. Hell, you could even go for a retro-inspired scheme and use this for trim and details in place of gold; it’d probably look lovely.

  • Yellow Details

    • Basecoat: Averland Sunset
    • Recess Shade: Fuegan Orange
    • Edge Highlight: Yriel Yellow
    • Extreme Edge Highlight: Dorn Yellow

Step 9. Leather

Straps, holsters, and handles of weapons will often be leather, and I like a warm dark brown. Contrary to my normal techniques, I only have one edge highlight on here, but I’ll point you in the right direction for highlight #2.

  • Brown Leather

    • Basecoat: Rhinox Hide
    • All-Over Shade: Agrax Earthshade
    • Edge Highlight: Doombull Brown
    • Extreme Edge Highlight (not pictured): Skrag Brown

Step 10. Purity Seals

You will invariably have a few of these Good Boi Awards on your Marines, and I like to give them a magenta hue to keep them distinct from red details. Sometimes I also use the Purity Seal Wax technique on weapon hilts if I’m feeling spicy. I keep the scrolls desaturated to help them stand out from any robes, and this technique also works well for any other scrollwork they may have.

  • Purity Seal Wax

    • Basecoat: Screamer Pink
    • All-Over Shade: Druchii Violet
    • Edge Highlight: Pink Horror
    • Extreme Edge Highlight: Emperor’s Children
  • Purity Seal Scroll

    • Basecoat: Rakarth Flesh
    • All-Over Shade: 1:1 mix of Nuln Oil and Agrax Earthshade
    • Edge Highlight: Rakarth Flesh
    • Extreme Edge Highlight: Pallid Wych Flesh

Step 11. Lenses

I’ll outline two techniques here - one for general red lenses, and one for green lenses whenever you have a lens appearing up against something red, such as the sergeant’s helmet. These will both usually be on eyes, but also on any targeters, monocles, and whatnot. I paint the eye the base color, then paint progressively brighter half moons towards the inside edge of the eye, then dot the outside, darker edge with pure white. 

  • Red Lenses

    • Basecoat: Mephiston Red
    • All-Over Shade: Nuln Oil
    • Edge Highlight: Evil Sunz Scarlet
    • Extreme Edge Highlight (inner): Fire Dragon Bright
    • Extreme Edge Highlight (outer): Pro Acryl Titanium White
  • Green Lenses

    • Basecoat: Caliban Green
    • All-Over Shade:  Nuln Oil
    • Edge Highlight: Warboss Green
    • Extreme Edge Highlight (inner): Skarsnik Green
    • Extreme Edge Highlight (outer): Pro Acryl Titanium White

Step 12. Robes

There won’t always be robes on models, so I saved this for last. If you wanted to, I’d probably get this step done before Step 9, as leather details and purity seals are often sitting on top of robes. I was still nailing my technique for robes at the time I painted these guys, but it was a pretty simple base, shade, and layer up. Nowadays, I would have blended between the base color and the layer instead of going straight from one to the next without a transition, but you can follow my guide or learn from my mistakes. I would also add a final edge highlight. 

  • Robes

    • Basecoat: Warhammer Zandri Dust
    • Recess Shade: Warhammer Agrax Earthshade
    • Layer: Warhammer Ushabti Bone
    • Highlight: Warhammer Wraithbone
    • Extreme Edge Highlight (not pictured): Warhammer Pallid Wych Flesh

Step 12. Transfers

No self-respecting Ultramarine would go to war without the proper iconography. My technique is identical to JD’s. However, we have one more step to go!

Step 13. Weathering

Transfers look great, and they look great when they’re a little scuffed up. For this, you’ll need a bit of foam because we’re going to do some sponge weathering. I have plenty of leftover hunks of foam plucked out of army cases over the years, so I rip a bit off, dip it in Rhinox Hide, dab some off on a paper towel, then start sponging the armored parts of the model. If you spill over onto any parts you don’t want to hit, if you’re quick and have a wet brush you can erase it. After sponging these armor chips brown, I use a fine brush with Stormhost Silver to define those chips in their biggest splotches. 

  • Chipping

    • Sponge: Warhammer Rhinox Hide
    • Highlight: Warhammer Stormhost Silver

I also will utilize a bit of weathering powder on the vents of each Marine’s power pack. I just jam an old brush full of black weathering powder onto the vents. I use Secret Weapon (RIP) Exhaust Black, but Mig Ammo Black would also do the trick.

  • Exhaust

    • Apply: Exhaust Black Weathering Powder

Step 14. Varnish

Any time you’re using transfers, weathering powders, or just painting over metal, you should varnish. Hell, you should probably do it on plastic models too. Varnish everything. I use Citadel’s Munitorum Varnish. Smarter Goonhammer writers than I have written many words on varnishing. Once you have this coat down, your models should be ready to go!

Campbell's 2nd Edition Ultramarines - Click to Expand

I have a retro Ultramarines army where no model is newer than 1997. I went for a "red period" 'Eavy Metal-style paint scheme with them, which you can follow below. As before, I won't tell you how to base your models, but I do have an up-to-date Goblin Green bases tutorial to complement these.

Funnily enough, a few of the colors and techniques here are nearly identical to those in my Primaris scheme. I'll reproduce them here anyway.

Step 1. Basecoat

We’re going to start with a basecoat of Skull White spray, although any white spray primer will do. I then spray with Army Painter Crystal Blue. It has a tendency to rub off; especially on metal models, so you'll likely want that white layer first. This is also more saturated than the Oldhammer look, but I had some grog in the Oldhammer group on Facebook cuss me out for not drybrushing the bases yellow and using too coarse basing grit. He's probably dead now.

Step 2. Blue Armor

It's a good idea to paint the whole model with thinned blue to ensure an even coat. Even moreso than with the modern look; going for a clean look is paramount. Always be ready to clean up after the fact.

  • Blue Armor

    • Basecoat: Army Painter Crystal Blue
    • Recess Shade: Warhammer Drakenhof Nightshade
    • Edge Highlight: Warhammer Calgar Blue
    • Extreme Edge Highlight: Warhammer Fenrisian Grey

Step 3. Yellow Armor Details

This is essentially a full shift upwards in brightness from my modern yellow technique, going for a warm, saturated yellow. This is also what I'd do for hazard stripes.

  • Yellow Details

    • Basecoat: Warhammer Yriel Yellow
    • Recess Shade: Warhammer Fuegan Orange
    • Edge Highlight: Warhammer Flash Gitz Yellow
    • Extreme Edge Highlight: Warhammer Dorn Yellow

Step 4. Red Armor and Weapon Casings

I usually paint these separately from the rest of the model, tacked onto a spare base or glued onto a thumbtack. Ideally, these are primed white with the rest of the model so you aren't painting so much red over blue.

  • Red Details

    • Basecoat: Warhammer Mephiston Red
    • Recess Shade: Warhammer Nuln Oil
    • Edge Highlight: Warhammer Wild Rider Red
    • Extreme Edge Highlight: Warhammer Fire Dragon Bright

Step 5. Steel

There isn't too much silver/steel on these guys; metallics weren't used as commonly then. If I were to do these again I'd probably go up to Ironbreaker instead of Leadbelcher for a brighter look. 

  • Steel

    • Basecoat: Warhammer Leadbelcher
    • All-Over Shade: Warhammer Nuln Oil
    • Edge Highlight: Warhammer Stormhost Silver

Step 6. Black Undersuit, Weapons, and Armor

Again, the undersuit and bolter stocks will be painted black, highlighted grey. I went for a neutral grey because I had to have at least one color on these models refrain from punching you in the face.

  • Black Details

    • Basecoat: P3 Thamar Black 
    • Edge Highlight: Warhammer Eshin Grey
    • Extreme Edge Highlight: Warhammer Dawnstone

Step 7. Lenses

These too are reproduced from my Primaris Marines scheme. It's almost like I painted these first and carried over a lot of the techniques!

  • Red Lenses

    • Basecoat: Warhammer Mephiston Red
    • All-Over Shade: Warhammer Nuln Oil
    • Edge Highlight: Warhammer Evil Sunz Scarlet
    • Extreme Edge Highlight (inner): Warhammer Fire Dragon Bright
    • Extreme Edge Highlight (outer): Pro Acryl Titanium White
  • Green Lenses

    • Basecoat: Warhammer Caliban Green
    • All-Over Shade: Warhammer Nuln Oil
    • Edge Highlight: Warhammer Warboss Green
    • Extreme Edge Highlight (inner): Warhammer Skarsnik Green
    • Extreme Edge Highlight (outer): Pro Acryl Titanium White

Step 8. Purity Seals

These were rarer back in the 90s, so I didn't paint as many, but they still showed up occasionally. I also did this technique for the skull on the heavy bolter Marine's kneepad.

  • Purity Seal Wax

    • Basecoat: Warhammer Mephiston Red
    • All-Over Shade: Warhammer Nuln Oil
    • Edge Highlight: Warhammer Wazdakka Red
    • Extreme Edge Highlight: Warhammer Wild Rider Red
  • Purity Seal Scroll

    • Basecoat: Warhammer Zandri Dust
    • All-Over Shade: Warhammer Agrax Earthshade
    • Layer: Warhammer Ushabti Bone
    • Edge Highlight: Warhammer Pallid Wych Flesh

Step 9. Transfers and Varnish

These are going to be the same as anybody else's steps, including my own. Get transfers on these models (or in my case, freehand and moulded pauldrons), then varnish away! Metal models chip super easily, especially if you don't have a really durable primer on them.

There's really just one special unit for the Ultramarines who needs his own article, and that's the Ultramarines' Primarch, Roboute Guilliman. You can find our article on How to Paint Roboute Guilliman here.

Final Thoughts

The Ultramarines may be the Boy Scouts of the Adeptus Astartes, but they're far from boring, with lots of unique characters and opportunities for interesting heraldry and special elements like laurel wreaths and cloth. They're a rewarding faction to paint and play, and unique in that regardless of what model you buy, you can always reference the box art for an example of a well-painted model.

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.

title: Steve Jackson Steps Down as CEO After 46 Years
content:
Steve Jackson is handing over the reins. The founder of Steve Jackson Games is stepping down as CEO after leading the company for 46 years, returning to what he’s always loved most: designing games.

Sabrina Gonzalez, a longtime SJG staffer, is taking over as CEO. Allison Page, previously Managing Editor, has been promoted to Chief Operating Officer.

The news was announced Friday, September 11, 2026, via press release and a follow-up post on the company’s blog, the Daily Illuminator. SJG is inviting fans to drop by their forums and congratulate both Gonzalez and Page on their new roles.

The End of an Era

Jackson founded SJG in 1980 after several years at Metagaming, and his fingerprints are all over the tabletop hobby. He created GURPS (Generic Universal Role Playing System) in 1983 — a genre-agnostic RPG now in its fourth edition, which Jackson and line editor Sean Punch have continually refined over the decades.

Other staples from his design career include the party favourite Munchkin, the quick-playing Zombie Dice, and the sci-fi wargame Ogre.

Jackson ran the company with an unusual degree of transparency, publishing yearly “report to stakeholders” blog posts. But SJG has struggled to keep pace with the wider industry in recent years — a challenge reflected in both its public-facing identity and its ability to pull in new customers. Modern players tend to gravitate toward either experimental indie titles or established giants like D&D and Pathfinder.

Jackson was always a designer first and a business owner out of necessity. Handing the CEO role to Gonzalez may give the company room to get back to what it does best.

Who Is Sabrina Gonzalez?

Gonzalez joined SJG in 2013 and has been with the company ever since, aside from a brief 2025 detour into game manufacturing that broadened her view of that side of the business. She’s held roles including Production Artist and Production Manager, and has sat on the company’s Board of Directors since 2021.

As for her goals, she’s thinking about both the future and the past. “As a general goal, I’d like us to continue to grow,” she said. “We weathered the pandemic and pivoted project plans to address continually changing tariffs. The goal is always to make great games that people love. I want to continue developing new titles for future generations of gamers and also support (and sometimes update) the classics that our fans continue to request.”

That dual approach is already taking shape. SJG recently struck a deal with Possum Creek Games to publish and sell its RPG catalogue, including Wanderhome and Yazeba’s Bed & Breakfast, bringing on Jay Dragon as lead game designer and Ruby Lavin as art director. The company has also licensed indie RPGs like Luke Jordan’s Grand Guignol and Caro Acersion’s Last Train to Bremen.

Away from the desk, Gonzalez is a fan of party and dice games — dominoes is her all-time favourite and travels with her. She’s also a multi-instrumentalist who plays guitar, piano, ukulele, and more.

One of her fondest SJG memories: one of her first assignments was designing everything for the Munchkin Tavern, from the logo to the signage and menus. A photo of the 2013 Tavern logo ended up on a T-shirt signed by many attendees that year — a memento that reminds her of good times with people who are no longer with us. “We still think of and miss you greatly, Andrew Hackard,” she said.

Who Is Allison Page?

Page joined SJG in 2023 as Managing Editor. Before that, she was Executive Artistic Director of Killing My Lobster, a San Francisco sketch comedy outfit, and worked as a Narrative Designer in video games — her entry point into the industry.

Like Gonzalez, Page gravitates toward party games. She describes herself as fiercely competitive and happy to take any excuse to shout and laugh. She’s been a comedy writer and playwright for over a decade, spending much of her time writing, reading others’ work in her writing group, and hanging out with fellow writers complaining about writing — which she considers a crucial part of the craft.

What’s Next for SJG

A few things are already in motion:

  • Steve Jackson will focus on game design and development. No specific projects have been announced yet.
  • Dragon’s 7 Part Pact — a complex RPG about wizards governing an archipelago through baroque politics and a shaky balance of occult power — recently raised over $1,000,000 from nearly 5,800 backers. Fulfillment and retail are currently estimated for late 2027.
  • Munchkin 5.5E RPG, designed in partnership with Lynnvander Studios, is expected to hit Backerkit next month.

Both Gonzalez and Page say they’re ready for the challenge and looking forward to ushering in a new era for the company.

title: D&D Delves Back Into the Underdark With New Playtest Options
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released a second round of Underdark-themed playtest material for Dungeons & Dragons, and it’s packed with new ways to build a character from the deep places of the world.

The new Unearthed Arcana: Underdark Options 2 PDF introduces three subclasses and five new species, all drawing on the strange, dangerous corners of D&D’s most storied subterranean setting. The survey opens on D&D Beyond starting September 17, so there’s time to test these options at your table before weighing in.

Three New Subclasses

The playtest features a mix of brand-new concepts and one returning favourite:

  • Freedom Domain (Cleric) — A high-Dexterity Cleric built around liberation, movement, and breaking chains. Its spell list was designed with a single question in mind: would this spell help in a jailbreak? Channel Divinity lets allies shake off conditions like Frightened, Grappled, Paralyzed, or Restrained and reposition without provoking opportunity attacks.
  • Circle of Spores (Druid) — An update to the subclass originally from Guildmaster’s Guide to Ravnica and Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, now tuned for 5.5e. The Underdark version leans harder into the myconid connection, granting Telepathy and reworking the old Spreading Spores feature into Explosive Burst — which makes your zombies detonate in a cloud of damaging spores when they die.
  • Faerzress Sorcery (Sorcerer) — Built around faerzress, the weird magical radiation of the Underdark. This Sorcerer can create zones of faerzress, ignore its drawbacks, and eventually transform into a being of pure faerzress energy. Lightning damage is the subclass’s signature flavour.

Five New Species

The species lineup is where things get really interesting. Rather than playing visitors from the surface, these options let you play characters who already call the Underdark home:

  • Deep Imaskari — Descendants of humans who fled into the depths millennia ago, now infused with the magic of “Unlight.” They create light rather than relying on Darkvision, and gain a versatile Aura of Unlight at level 3.
  • Drider — The classic drow-spider hybrid, finally playable. You get Spider Climb, Web Walker, and spells of the Spider Queen, with mechanics inspired by the Centaur from Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse.
  • Illithidkin — Victims (or willing participants) of mind flayer experimentation. They get psionic abilities, Psychic resistance, and telepathy. Notably, this is a separate route from the Ceremorphosis feat path in the previous UA, not meant to be combined with it.
  • Kuo-toa — Fishlike humanoids with a talent for creating bizarre, sometimes living idols. Their Deific Manifestation feature lets you cast Find Familiar and mix and match traits from two different forms to build your own little abomination.
  • Myconid — Bipedal fungal folk and the ultimate team players. Their abilities focus on building rapport, sharing knowledge, and granting the whole party telepathy through spores.

What the Design Team Is Saying

Senior Game Designer Jason Tondro noted that this UA touches on elements of the Underdark that have appeared before but are being “expanded or transformed in ways we’re not yet ready to fully reveal.” Faerzress, for example, dates back to 1978’s D1 Descent into the Depths of the Earth, while the Deep Imaskari first appeared in 2003’s Underdark supplement.

The material uses the Player’s Handbook rules, and Wizards is clear that these options are experimental — they may end up more or less powerful than what’s currently in the game, and could change significantly before any official publication.

How to Get Involved

If you want to help shape what makes it into a future D&D book, now’s your chance. Try these subclasses and species in your campaign or a one-shot, then fill out the survey on D&D Beyond when it goes live on September 17.

Worth noting: the document includes a content warning for body horror and mind control, so keep that in mind depending on your table.

title: Discworld Returns to the Tabletop with New Modiphius RPG
content:
Modiphius Entertainment is heading back to the Disc — and this time it’s trading the cobbled streets of Ankh-Morpork for the hills, forests, and castles of the Ramtops.

The publisher has announced Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald, a brand-new tabletop RPG launching on Gamefound this October. It follows the success of Discworld: Adventures in Ankh Morpork, which raised over £2m on Kickstarter during its 2025 campaign.

A Standalone Trip to the Ramtops

The good news for newcomers: you won’t need the first book to jump in. Adventures in Lancre and Überwald is a standalone core rulebook, playable with or without its predecessor. That makes it an easy entry point for anyone who’s been curious about Discworld roleplaying but didn’t back the original campaign.

The new book explores three iconic corners of Terry Pratchett’s world:

  • Lancre — home turf of the witches
  • Überwald — the gloomy, vampire-heavy region beyond the mountains
  • The Chalk — the rural downland region introduced in the later Discworld novels

Play as Witches, Vampires, Trolls, and Werewolves

Players will be able to encounter — and play as — witches, vampires, trolls, and werewolves, opening up a much wider range of character options than before. The book also brings in plenty of fan-favourite characters and locations, from the Ogg clan to Don’tgonearthe Castle to Granny Weatherwax herself.

For the first time in the official Discworld RPG line, there are also full rules for running ongoing campaigns, plus a book of linked adventures that takes players on a tour of the Ramtops.

What’s in the Campaign

Modiphius is promising a hefty spread of options when the Gamefound campaign goes live in October, including:

  • A hardcover core rulebook in standard and collector’s editions
  • An adventure book
  • A GM Toolkit
  • Additional supplements
  • Dice

The publisher is also putting extra focus on onboarding. The book includes expanded guidance and support for new players and gamemasters, with more examples that lean into the humour and wit Pratchett’s series is known for. There are also expanded rules for complex challenges, new risks for taking multiple consequences, and plenty of common situations explained in full — all of which Modiphius is billing as the easiest entry point yet for newcomers to both Discworld and tabletop RPGs in general.

More Discworld on the Way

This isn’t the only Discworld project in Modiphius’s pipeline. The publisher also has Kill Sam Vimes, a light board game about pursuing the titular character, and Readers Digested, a licensed edition of Reiner Knizia’s Blue Moon City, both available to pre-order now.

The Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald Gamefound campaign launches in October.

title: Wizards of the Coast Releases Exodus TTRPG, Tying Into Upcoming Sci-Fi Video Game

Wizards of the Coast has released Exodus, a new sci-fi tabletop RPG set in the same universe as the upcoming AAA video game from Archetype Entertainment. The Traveler’s Handbook and Exodus Encyclopedia are now available for purchase through the official Exodus webpage.

Both books are full-color hardcovers with Smythe sewn binding and spot UV finishing. The project also features contributions from award-winning sci-fi authors Adrian Tchaikovsky and Peter F. Hamilton.

The Exodus video game is slated for release in 2026 on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S.

title: CMON Faces Make-or-Break Moment as It Warns of “Prolonged Structural Downturn”
content:
CMON has issued a stark warning about its future, telling investors its core business is stuck in a “prolonged structural downturn” and still burning through more cash than it brings in. The tabletop crowdfunding giant is now racing to raise up to $17.5m from outside investors.

The warning landed alongside CMON’s H1 financial report, and it caps off a brutal 18 months for one of the biggest names in crowdfunded board games.

Parts of this article is based on info from BoardGameWire.

A Company Half Its Former Size

CMON has spent the past year and a half trying to stop the bleeding. The publisher has:

  • Cut its workforce in half
  • Sold off major IP including Zombicide, Blood Rage, and Cthulhu: Death May Die
  • Shut down its Singapore office
  • Halted new crowdfunding campaigns

Those moves have helped — but not enough to fix the underlying problem.

Losses Shrinking, But Cash Still Draining

The good news: CMON’s losses are shrinking fast.

The company posted a loss of just over $2m in the first half of 2026, compared to nearly $7m during the same stretch last year. Revenue also crept up more than 7% year-on-year, hitting $3.68m. Selling and distribution costs were cut by more than half, and administrative expenses dropped from $4.37m to $2.37m.

The bad news: it’s still not enough to keep the lights on without outside help.

CMON’s cash reserves have been in freefall. They sat at $3.9m at the end of 2022, fell to $2.1m by the end of 2024, and slipped to just over $900,000 by June 2025. In early August, the company revealed it had roughly $368,000 on hand — less than a month’s worth of operating expenses.

The Backer Problem: $14m in Undelivered Games

A huge chunk of CMON’s financial pressure comes down to games that backers have already paid for but haven’t received.

Eight crowdfunded titles remain undelivered, representing $14m raised from backers. The two biggest are **DC Super Heroes United** (over $4.4m raised) and DCeased (over $2.5m). Both were originally due last year, but have been delayed repeatedly and are now slated for Q1 2027.

CMON hasn’t completed fulfillment on a crowdfunding project since Zombicide: White Death in mid-2025. It has managed to ship some pre-orders — Cthulhu: Dark Providence, Marvel United: Witching Hour, and Dune: Desert War all went out in the first half of this year — but four more pre-order titles remain in limbo, including the Assassin’s Creed Role Playing Game.

The $17.5m Gamble

To stay afloat, CMON is leaning on a massive rights issue designed to raise up to HK$150.5m (about $19m). The plan lets existing shareholders buy three new shares for every one they already own.

There’s just one problem: shareholders barely took the bait. Only 7.76% of the new shares were claimed by the August deadline, leaving CMON scrambling to find more than $17.5m from other investors — a figure approaching 2.5-times the company’s entire valuation from its last share sale in February.

If the money comes through, here’s how CMON plans to spend it:

  • 40% — Day-to-day operations for roughly a year, including staff, royalties, shipping, and distribution
  • 20% — Paying down debts, including $2.46m owed to a company director and $385,000 in unsecured employee advances
  • 25% — Expansion into existing and new markets, with a focus on Europe, Japan, and the Philippines
  • 15% — Potential acquisitions in digital gaming

The final result of the rights issue is due September 15.

A Digital Pivot — With a Catch

That 15% digital acquisition budget is notable, especially since CMON just walked away from a planned $2.1m investment in NFT game maker Blissful Link. That deal would have valued Blissful Link at over $95m — despite the company posting a loss of about $197,000 in 2024 on revenues of just over $408,000.

CMON says it’s now hunting for one to three businesses, mostly in Asia-Pacific, valued between $1.3m and $2.5m each, to help build digital adaptations and companion apps. The publisher insists physical tabletop games remain its core business and that digital is meant to complement, not replace, them.

Where the Money Comes From Now

The report also lays bare just how dramatically CMON’s geographic revenue has shifted.

North America generated over $8.6m in the first half of 2021 — 57% of the company’s roughly $15.1m revenue at the time. By the first half of 2026, North and South America combined brought in just $642,000.

Europe has collapsed similarly, falling from about $4.5m to $982,000 over the same period.

Asia is now CMON’s largest market by a wide margin, generating over $2m and accounting for about 55% of total revenue — up from less than 10% in 2021. That’s not because Asia is growing, though. Revenue there is down roughly 37% since 2022. It’s just fallen far less than everywhere else.

What’s Next for Crowdfunding?

CMON said back in March that it intended to resume crowdfunding in the second half of 2026. Its latest report doesn’t repeat that promise. Instead, the company says new titles will be developed and launched “selectively” based on market conditions, available cash, and project readiness.

For a publisher built on the crowdfunding model, that’s a notable shift in tone — and a sign that CMON’s road back to stability is still a long one.
